---
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
Let $\mathscr{C}$ be a locally presentable, closed symmetric monoidal category.
Let $F\colon \mathscr{C}\rightarrow \mathscr{C}$ be an accessible, lax symmetric monoidal functor. 
Then the category of $F$-algebras in $\mathscr{C}$ is enriched, tensored and cotensored over the closed symmetric monoidal category of $F$-coalgebras in $\mathscr{C}$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
Consider the polynomial ring $\mathbb{R}[x]$ which is an $\mathbb{R}$-algebra with the usual multiplication of polynomials.
 Consider the derivation operator 
 \begin{align*}
     D\colon \mathbb{R}[x] & \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}[x]\\
     f(x) & \longmapsto f'(x).
 \end{align*}
 This is a $\mathbb{R}$-linear homomorphism but not an $\mathbb{R}$-algebra homomorphism as $D(fg)\neq D(f)D(g)$ and $D(1)\neq 1$.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
Consider the multiplication by 2 on the rationals: $m_2\colon\mathbb{Q}\rightarrow\mathbb{Q}$ sending $a \mapsto 2a$ for all $a\in \mathbb{Q}$. It is a $\mathbb{Q}$-linear homomorphism but not an algebra homomorphism when $\mathbb{Q}$ is viewed as a $\mathbb{Q}$-algebra with its usual multiplication, as $m_2(ab)=2ab \neq 4ab = m_2(a)m_2(b)$.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- example-3: body_md -->
\label{ex:binomial}
The \emph{binomial} $k$-coalgebra structure on $k[x]$ is given by the comultiplication
\begin{align*}
   \Delta\colon  k[x] & \longrightarrow k[x]\otimes_k k[x]\\
   x^n & \longmapsto \sum_i \binom{n}{i} x^{n-i}\otimes x^{i} 
\end{align*}
and co-unit
\begin{align*}
    \varepsilon\colon k[x] & \longrightarrow k\\
    x^n & \longmapsto 0.
\end{align*}
<!-- end example-3 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
Given a $k$-coalgebra $C$ and a $k$-algebra $B$, we call $([C, B], \ast, 1_{[C,B]})$ the \emph{convolution algebra}\index{convolution algebra!over a field} of $C$ with $B$.
The construction is natural in $C$ and $B$ and defines a functor
\[
[-,-]\colon \mathrm{coAlg}_k^\mathrm{op}\times \mathrm{Alg}_k \longrightarrow \mathrm{Alg}_k.
\]
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- example-4: body_md -->
If we let $C=k$, the terminal $k$-coalgebra,  then the convolution algebra $[k, B]$ is isomorphic to $B$ as a $k$-algebra.
<!-- end example-4 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def: partial homomorphism}
Given $k$-algebras $A$ and $B$ and a $k$-coalgebra $C$, a $k$-linear homomorphism $\widetilde{f}\colon C\rightarrow [A,B]$ is called a \emph{$C$-indexed partial homomorphism from $A$ to $B$}\index{partial homomorphism indexed over a coalgebra!over a field} if its adjunct $\widehat{f}\colon A\rightarrow [C, B]$ is an algebra homomorphism. 
Denoting $\gls{partialhm}\coloneqq \widetilde{f}(c)$ 
for all $c\in C$, this means that for all $x,y\in A$ we have
\[
f_c(xy)=\sum_{(c)}f_{c_{(1)}}(x) f_{c_{(2)}}(y) \quad \quad \quad  f_c(1_A)=\varepsilon(c)1_B.
\]
In other words, we obtain the following commutative diagrams in vector spaces
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep= large]
    C\ar{r}{\Delta} \ar{d}[swap]{\widetilde{f}}& C\otimes_k C \ar{r}{\widetilde{f}\otimes \widetilde{f}} & {[A,B]\otimes_k [A,B]} \ar{r}{\nabla} & {[A\otimes_k A, B\otimes_k B]} \ar{d}{{\mu_B}_*}\\
    {[A,B]} \ar{rrr}{\mu_A^*} &&& {[A\otimes_k A, B]}
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
    C \ar{rr}{\widetilde{f}} \ar{d}[swap]{\varepsilon} & [-2em] & {[A,B]}\ar{d}{{\eta_B}_*}\\
    k \ar[phantom, "\cong"]{r}&  {[k,k]} \ar{r}{\eta_A^*} & {[A,k]}.
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Here, $\nabla$ is the transformation
\begin{align*}
\nabla\colon [V_1, V_2]\otimes_k [V_3, V_4]& \longrightarrow [V_1 \otimes_k V_3, V_2 \otimes_k V_4]\\
f \otimes g & \longmapsto f\otimes g
\end{align*}
natural in vector spaces $V_1$, $V_2$, $V_3$ and $V_4$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
A $C$-indexed partial homomorphism is \emph{not} a partial function. It is a function that should be regarded as only partially multiplicative. Indeed, a homomorphism is multiplicative function, therefore, the term partial homomorphism should not be confused with the notion of partial function.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- example-5: body_md -->
Choose $C=\mathbb{R}[x]$ and $A,B=\mathbb{R}[x]$ as in \cref{ex:binomial}.    We can view the derivation $D\colon \mathbb{R}[x]\rightarrow \mathbb{R}[x]$ as an $\mathbb{R}[x]$-indexed partial homomorphism
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{R}[x] & \longrightarrow [\mathbb{R}[x], \mathbb{R}[x]]\\
    x^n & \longmapsto D^n.
\end{align*}
We have $\Delta(x)=x\otimes 1 + 1\otimes x$, and so we recover the formula 
\[
D(fg)=D(f)g+fD(g),
\]
and more generally
\[
D^n(fg)=\sum_{i=0}^n \binom{n}{i} D^{n-i}(f)D^{i}(g).
\]
<!-- end example-5 -->
<!-- example-6: body_md -->
We can view $\mathbb{Q}$ as a coalgebra over itself via $\mathbb{Q}\stackrel{\cong}\rightarrow \mathbb{Q}\otimes_\mathbb{Q}\mathbb{Q}$  defined by $q\mapsto q\otimes 1$.  
 We have a $\mathbb{Q}$-indexed partial homomorphism 
 \begin{align*}
     \mathbb{Q} &\longrightarrow [\mathbb{Q}, \mathbb{Q}]\\
     q & \longmapsto m_q
 \end{align*}
 where $m_q(a)=qa$. 
 The partial homomorphism says that \[m_q(ab)=q(ab)= (qa)b=m_q(a)m_1(b).\]
<!-- end example-6 -->
<!-- example-7: body_md -->
Building on the previous example, given any $k$-algebra homomorphism $f\colon A\rightarrow B$, choose the trivial $k$-coalgebra structure on $k$ via $\Delta\colon k\stackrel{\cong}\rightarrow k\otimes_k k$, and define a $k$-partial homomorphism
\begin{align*}
    k& \longrightarrow [A,B]\\
    q  & \longmapsto f_q
\end{align*}
where  $f_q(x)=qf(x)$ for all $x\in A$  and $q\in k$.
As $\Delta(1)=1\otimes 1$, we get:
\[
f(xy)=f_1(xy)=f_1(x)f_1(y)=f(x)f(y),
\]
recovering the fact that $f$ is an algebra homomorphism. 
We obtain in fact a correspondence between algebra homomorphisms $A\rightarrow B$ and $k$-partial homomorphisms $k\rightarrow [A,B]$.
<!-- end example-7 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def: measurings}
Given $k$-algebras $A$ and $B$ and a $k$-coalgebra $C$, a $k$-linear homomorphism $f\colon C\otimes_k A\rightarrow B$ is called
\emph{a $C$-measuring of $A$ and $B$}\index{measuring of algebras!over a field} if its adjunct $\widetilde{f}\colon C\rightarrow [A,B]$ is a $C$-indexed partial homomorphism, or equivalently, the other adjoint $\widehat{f}\colon A\rightarrow [C, B]$ is an algebra homomorphism.
This means that for all $c\in C$ and $x,y\in A$, we have
\[
f(c\otimes xy)=\sum_{(c)} f(c_{(1)}\otimes x) f(c_{(2)}\otimes y), \quad  \quad f(c\otimes 1_A)=\varepsilon(c)1_B.
\]
In other words, we have the following commutative diagrams in vector spaces:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large]
    C\otimes_k A^{\otimes 2} \ar{d}[swap]{1\otimes \mu_A}\ar{r}{\Delta \otimes 1} & C^{\otimes 2}\otimes_k A^{\otimes 2} \ar[phantom, "\cong"]{r}& [-2em] (C\otimes_k A)^{\otimes 2} \ar{r}{f\otimes f} & B\otimes_k B \ar{d}{\mu_B}\\
    C\otimes_k A \ar{rrr}{f} & & & B
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
    C\otimes_k k \ar{d}[swap]{1\otimes \eta_A} \ar[phantom, "\cong"]{r}& [-2em] C \ar{r}{\varepsilon} & k \ar{d}{\eta_B}\\
    C\otimes_k A \ar{rr}{f} & & B.
\end{tikzcd}
\]
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{def: measuring functor to set}
Let $A$, $B$ be $k$-algebras and $C$ a $k$-coalgebra.
Let \gls{MeasuringSet} be the set of $C$-measurings $C\otimes_k A\rightarrow B$ of $A$ to $B$, or equivalently, the set of $C$-indexed partial homomorphisms $C\rightarrow [A, B]$. 
Given a measuring $f\colon C\otimes_k A\rightarrow B$, a coalgebra homomorphism $c\colon C'\rightarrow C$, and algebra homomorphisms $a\colon A'\rightarrow A$ and $b\colon B\rightarrow B'$, we obtain a new $C$-measuring $f'\colon C'\otimes_k A'\rightarrow B'$ as the composite
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
C'\otimes_k A' \ar{r}{c\otimes a} & C\otimes_k A \ar{r}{f} & B \ar{r}{b} & B'. 
\end{tikzcd}
\]
By doing this for any such $f$, we obtain a function $\mu_C(A,B)\rightarrow \mu_{C'}(A',B')$.
This makes $\mu$ into a functor
                                                                 
\begin{align*}
    \mu\colon \mathrm{coAlg}_k^\mathrm{op}\times \mathrm{Alg}_k^\mathrm{op} \times \mathrm{Alg} & \longrightarrow \mathrm{Set}\\
    (C, A, B) & \longmapsto \mu_C(A,B).
\end{align*}
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
\label{def: universal measuring}
Given $k$-algebras $A$ and $B$, denote by $(\gls{UnivMeasuring}, \widetilde{\mathrm{ev}})$ the terminal object (if it exists) of the category $\mathscr{M}(A,B)$ of measurings from $A$ to $B$. The coalgebra $\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}_k(A, B)$ is called the \emph{universal measuring coalgebra}\index{universal measuring coalgebra!over a field}
                                                                                                         
from $A$ to $B$ and its measuring $\mathrm{ev}\colon\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}_k(A, B)\otimes_k  A\rightarrow B$ is called the \emph{evaluation}. 
This means given an $C$-indexed partial homomorphisms $\widetilde{f}\colon C\rightarrow [A, B]$,  there exists a unique coalgebra homomorphism $u_f\colon C\rightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Alg}}_k(A, B)$ such that the following diagram commutes:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
    C \ar{r}{\widetilde{f}} \ar[dashed]{d}[swap]{\exists! u_f}& {[A, B]}\\
\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}_k(A, B). \ar[bend right]{ur}[swap]{\widetilde{\mathrm{ev}}}
\end{tikzcd}
\]
The construction is natural in $A$ and $B$ and defines a functor
\[
\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}_k(-, -)\colon \mathrm{Alg}_k^\mathrm{op}\times \mathrm{Alg}_k \longrightarrow \mathrm{coAlg}_k.
\]
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
Given $k$-algebras $A$ and $B$, the measuring coalgebra $(\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}_k(A, B), \widetilde{\mathrm{ev}})$ exists and is determined by the following equalizer in $\mathrm{coAlg}_k$
 \[
 \begin{tikzcd}
     \underline{\mathrm{Alg}}_k(A, B) \ar[dashed]{r}{\overline{\mathrm{ev}}} & T^\vee ([A, B]) \ar[shift left  =1]{r}{\Phi}\ar[shift right =1]{r}[swap]{\Psi} &  T^\vee\left([A^{\otimes 2}, B]\right)\oplus T^\vee([A, k]).
 \end{tikzcd}
 \]
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- example-8: body_md -->
Given a $k$-coalgebra $(C, \Delta, \varepsilon)$, a grouplike element in  $C$ is an element $g\in C$ such that $\Delta(g)=g\otimes g$ and $\varepsilon(g)=1$.  
 The set of grouplike elements in $C$ is in bijective correspondence with coalgebra homomorphisms $k\rightarrow C$.
 Applying this to a universal measuring $C=\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}_k(A, B)$ we obtain
 \[
 \mathrm{coAlg}_k(k, \underline{\mathrm{Alg}}_k(A, B))\cong \mathrm{Alg}_k(A, [k, B])\cong \mathrm{Alg}_k(A, B).
 \]
 Therefore, the set of grouplike elements of $\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}_k(A, B)$ is precisely the hom-set of  algebra homomorphisms $A\rightarrow B$.
<!-- end example-8 -->
<!-- example-9: body_md -->
Given a $k$-coalgebra $(C, \Delta, \varepsilon)$ and a grouplike element $g\in C$, a \emph{primitive element over $g$} of $C$ is an element $d\in C$ such that $\Delta(d)=d\otimes g+ g\otimes d$.
Given a $C$-partial homomorphism $\widetilde{f}\colon C\rightarrow [A,B]$, we obtain for all $x,y\in A$
\[
f_d(xy)=f_d(x)f_g(y)+f_g(x)f_d(y).
\]
Here, $f_g\colon A\to B$ is an algebra  homomorphism by the previous example, and thus $f_d\colon A\rightarrow B$ is a derivation from $A$ to $B$.  Therefore, the set of primitive elements of $\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}_k(A, B)$ is the set of derivations $A\rightarrow B$.
<!-- end example-9 -->
<!-- example-10: body_md -->
Given a vector space $V$ and an algebra $B$, we obtain an isomorphism of coalgebras:
\[
\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}_k(T(V), B) \cong T^\vee([V ,B]).
\]
This is due to the fact that for any coalgebra $C$ we have the series of invertible linear maps
\begin{align*}
  \mathrm{coAlg}_k(C,  \underline{\mathrm{Alg}}_k(T(V), B)) & \cong \mathrm{Alg}_k(T(V), [C, B])\\
  & \cong \mathrm{Vect}_k(V, [C, B])\\
  & \cong \mathrm{Vect}_k(C, [V, B])\\
  & \cong \mathrm{coAlg}_k(C, T^\vee([V, B])).
\end{align*}
<!-- end example-10 -->
<!-- example-11: body_md -->
Given a $k$-coalgebra $C$ and a $k$-algebra $A$, we can view $k$ as both a $k$-algebra and $k$-coalgebra, and we obtain a bijection
\[
\mathrm{coAlg}_k(C, \underline{\mathrm{Alg}}_k(A, k))\cong \mathrm{Alg}_k(A, [C, k]).
\]
The $k$-algebra $C^*\coloneqq [C, k]$ is called the \emph{dual algebra of $C$}, and the $k$-coalgebra $A^\circ\coloneqq \underline{\mathrm{Alg}}_k(A, k)$ is called the \emph{finite dual} or \emph{Sweedler dual of $A$}.
We can check that in vector spaces, we have $A^\circ\cong A^*$ if and only if $A$ is finite dimensional.
We obtain natural identifications for all $C\in \mathrm{coAlg}_k$ and $A\in \mathrm{Alg}_k$:
    \[
    {\mathrm{Alg}}_k(A, C^*)\cong {\mathrm{coAlg}}_k(C, A^\circ).
    \]
<!-- end example-11 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
Given a $k$-coalgebra $C$ and $k$-algebra $A$, define $\mathscr{M}_C(A)$ to be the category whose objects consist of pairs $(B, f)$ where $B$ is a $k$-algebra and $f\colon C\otimes_k A\rightarrow B$ is a $C$-measuring.
 A morphism $(B_1, f_1)\rightarrow (B_2, f_2)$ in $\mathscr{M}_C(A)$ consists of an algebra homomorphism $\beta\colon B_1\rightarrow B_2$ such that the following diagram commutes.
 \[
 \begin{tikzcd}
  &  C\otimes_k A\ar{dr}{f_2} \ar{dl}[swap]{f_1} &\\
  B_1 \ar{rr}{\beta} & & B_2
 \end{tikzcd}
 \]
 Composition and identity on $\mathscr{M}_C(A)$ are induced from $\mathrm{Alg}_k$.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
Given a $k$-coalgebra $C$ and $k$-algebra $A$, denote by $(C\triangleright A, u)$ the initial object of the category $\mathscr{M}_C(A)$.
The $k$-algebra $\gls{MeasTens}$ is called \emph{the measuring tensor}\index{measuring tensor!over a field} of $C$ with $A$, and its measuring $u\colon C\otimes_k A\rightarrow C\triangleright A$ is called the universal measuring of $C$ with $A$.
This means given any $C$-measuring $f\colon C\otimes_k A\rightarrow B$, there exists a unique algebra homomorphism $C\triangleright A\rightarrow B$ such that:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
    C\otimes_k A \ar{r}{f} \ar{d}[swap]{u} &  B.\\
    C\triangleright A \ar[dashed]{ur}[swap]{\exists !}
\end{tikzcd}
\]
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm: measuring tensor as coequalizer}
 Given a $k$-algebra $B$ and a $k$-coalgebra $C$, the measuring tensor $(C\triangleright A, u)$ exists and is the following coequalizer in $\mathrm{Alg}_k$
 \[
\begin{tikzcd}
{T(C\otimes_k A^{\otimes 2})} \oplus T(C\otimes_k k) \ar[shift left  =1]{r}{\Phi}\ar[shift right =1]{r}[swap]{\Psi} &  T(C\otimes_k A)  \ar[dashed]{r}{u'}  & C\triangleright A.
\end{tikzcd}
\]
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
The existence of the measuring tensor was already known in \cite{Fox}.
    The notation $C\triangleright A$ first appeared in \cite{anel2013sweedler}.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
The measuring tensor induces a functor
\[
-\triangleright -\colon \mathrm{coAlg}_k \times \mathrm{Alg}_k \longrightarrow \mathrm{Alg}_k.
\]
It is useful to describe $C\triangleright A$ as follows. 
Given $c\in C$, and $x\in A$, and the universal measuring $u\colon C\otimes_k A\rightarrow C\triangleright A$,
put $c\triangleright x\coloneqq u(c\otimes x)$.
Then $C\triangleright A$ is the algebra generated by the symbols $c\triangleright x$ under the relations
\[
c\triangleright (xy) = \sum_{(c)}(c_{(1)}\triangleright x)(c_{(2)}\triangleright y), \quad \quad c\triangleright 1_A=\varepsilon(c)
\]
for all $c\in C$ and $x,y \in A$.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
\label{def: enriched category}
    Consider a monoidal category $(\mathscr{V}, \otimes, \mathbb I)$, the \emph{enriching} category \index{category enriched over a monoidal category}, and a category $\mathscr{C}$, the \emph{underlying} category.
We say that $\mathscr{C}$ has an \emph{enrichment} in $\mathscr{V}$ if there is a functor
    \[ \underline{\hom}_\mathscr{C}(-,-) \colon \mathscr{C}^\mathrm{op} \times \mathscr{C} \to \mathscr{V} \]
    together with the following.
    \begin{itemize}
        \par For each $A\in \mathscr{C}$, a morphism called the \emph{identity} on $A$:
        \[ \mathrm{id}_A\colon \mathbb I\rightarrow \underline{\hom}_\mathscr{C}(A,A).\] 
        \par For each $A, B, C\in \mathscr{C}$, a morphism in $\mathscr{V}$ called \emph{composition}
        \[
        \circ\colon \underline{\hom}_\mathscr{C}(B, C)\otimes \underline{\hom}_\mathscr{C}(A, B) \longrightarrow \underline{\hom}_\mathscr{C}(A, C).
        \]
        \par For each $A, B \in \mathscr{C}$, a bijection:
        \[ \hom_\mathscr{C} (A, B) \cong \hom_\mathscr{C} (\mathbb I, \underline{\hom}_{\mathscr{C}}(A,B)). \]
    \end{itemize}
    such that the standard associativity and unitality diagrams commute, all the above morphisms are (extra)natural in $A,B,C$, and such the identity and composition $\mathscr{V}$-morphisms are compatible with the identity and composition morphisms of $\mathscr{C}$.
We also call this structure a \emph{$\mathscr{V}$-enriched category}, and when we are considering $\mathscr{C}$ with this extra structure, we will sometimes write $\underline{\mathscr{C}}$. The notion was introduced in \cite{benabou1965categories}, see \cite{Kelly} for a standard reference.
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
It is more standard to define a $\mathscr{V}$-enriched category $\underline{\mathscr{C}}$ using only the first two bullet points, without introducing a category $\mathscr{C}$, and deducing an underlying category $\mathscr{C}$ using third bullet point. See more details in \cite{Kelly}.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- example-12: body_md -->
If $\mathscr{V}$ is a closed symmetric monoidal category, its internal hom, often denoted $\underline{\hom}_\mathscr{V}(-,-)$ determines $\mathscr{V}$ as enriched over itself.
<!-- end example-12 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm: alg enriched in coalg}
The category $\mathrm{Alg}_k$ of $k$-algebras is enriched in the closed symmetric monoidal category $(\mathrm{coAlg}_k, \otimes_k, k, \underline{\mathrm{coAlg}}_k(-,-))$ of $k$-coalgebras, for which the hom-coalgebra between two algebras $A$ and $B$ is given by the universal measuring $\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}_k(A, B)$. 
It is also tensored over $\mathrm{coAlg}_k$ via the measuring tensor and cotensored via the convolution algebra. In other words, we obtain the following natural isomorphisms in $\mathrm{coAlg}_k$:
\[
\underline{\mathrm{coAlg}}_k(C, \underline{\mathrm{Alg}}_k(A, B))\cong \underline{\mathrm{Alg}}_k(C\triangleright A, B) \cong \underline{\mathrm{Alg}}_k(A, [C,B]).
\]
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
The convolution algebra $[-,-]\colon \mathrm{coAlg}_k^\mathrm{op}\times \mathrm{Alg}_k \rightarrow \mathrm{Alg}_k$ determines $\mathrm{Alg}_k$ as a right module over $\mathrm{coAlg}_k^\mathrm{op}$, in the sense that we have the following natural isomorphisms in $\mathrm{Alg}_k$ for all coalgebras $C,D$ and algebra $A$
 \[
 [C\otimes_k D, A]\cong [C, [D,A]] \quad \quad [k, A]\cong A.
 \]
 Thus $\mathrm{Alg}_k^\mathrm{op}$ is a left module over $\mathrm{coAlg}_k$ via $[-,-]^\mathrm{op}\colon \mathrm{coAlg}_k\times \mathrm{Alg}_k^\mathrm{op}\rightarrow \mathrm{Alg}_k^\mathrm{op}$.
 Moreover, for any algebra $B$, the induced functor $[-,B]^\mathrm{op}\colon \mathrm{coAlg}_k\rightarrow \mathrm{Alg}_k^\mathrm{op}$ has a right adjoint $\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}_k(-, B)\colon \mathrm{Alg}_k^\mathrm{op}\rightarrow \mathrm{coAlg}_k$ as we have the natural isomorphism
 \[
 \mathrm{coAlg}_k(C, \underline{\mathrm{Alg}}_k(A, B))\cong \mathrm{Alg}_k(A, [C, B]). 
 \]
 By \cite[3.1]{hylandetal}, we obtain that $\mathrm{Alg}_k^\mathrm{op}$ is enriched, tensored and cotensored over $\mathrm{coAlg}_k$.
 Thus $\mathrm{Alg}_k$ is enriched, tensored and cotensored over $\mathrm{coAlg}_k$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{remark: coalgebras measurings and universal internal hom}
While $\mathrm{Alg}_k$ is enriched in $\mathrm{coAlg}_k$, we do not have that $\mathrm{coAlg}_k$ is enriched in $\mathrm{Alg}_k$. However, because $\mathrm{coAlg}_k$ is closed symmetric monoidal, it is enriched in itself. 
This actually also defines a notion of measurings and partial homomorphism for coalgebras as we can now define. 

Let $(C, \Delta, \varepsilon)$, $(C_1, \Delta_1, \varepsilon_1)$ and $(C_2, \Delta_2, \varepsilon_2)$ be $k$-coalgebras.
A \emph{$C$-measuring} from $C_1$ to $C_2$ is a homomorphism of coalgebras $f\colon C\otimes_k C_1\rightarrow C_2$. 
We say a map $\widetilde{f}\colon C\rightarrow [C_1, C_2]$ is a \emph{$C$-indexed partial homomorphism from $C_1$ to $C_2$} if its adjunct $C\otimes_k C_1\rightarrow C_2$ is a $C$-measuring. In other words, if we denote $f_c\coloneqq \widetilde{f}(c)$ for all $c\in C$, this means for all $x\in C_1$:
\[
\sum_{(f_c(x))} {f_c(x)}_{(1)}\otimes {f_c(x)}_{(2)}=\sum_{(x)}\sum_{(c)} f_{c_{(1)}}(x_{(1)})\otimes f_{c_{(2)}}(x_{(2)})
\]
and
\[
\varepsilon_2(f_c(x))=\varepsilon(c)\varepsilon_1(x).
\]
We see that $f_c\colon C_1\rightarrow C_2$ is a homomorphism of coalgebras if $c$ is a grouplike element.

With these notions, we interpret the internal hom $\underline{\mathrm{coAlg}}_k(C_1, C_2)$ as the universal measuring coalgebra from $C_1$ to  $C_2$, in the sense that, given any $C$-partial homomorphism $f\colon C\rightarrow [C_1, C_2]$,  there exists a unique homomorphism of coalgebras $u_f\colon C\rightarrow \underline{\mathrm{coAlg}}_k(C_1, C_2)$ such that the following diagram commutes:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
    C \ar{r}{f} \ar[dashed]{d}[swap]{\exists !\, u_f}& {[C_1, C_2]}\\
    \underline{\mathrm{coAlg}}_k(C_1, C_2).\ar{ur}
\end{tikzcd}
\]
This is making precise the natural identification
\[
\underline{\mathrm{coAlg}}_k(C\otimes_k C_1, C_2) \cong \underline{\mathrm{coAlg}}_k(C, \underline{\mathrm{coAlg}}_k(C_1, C_2))\cong \underline{\mathrm{coAlg}}_k(C_1, \underline{\mathrm{coAlg}}_k(C, C_2)).
\]
This is the coalgebraic analogue of \cref{thm: alg enriched in coalg}.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
Given an endofunctor $F$ on a category $\mathscr{C}$, an \emph{algebra} for $F$, or simply \emph{an $F$-algebra}\index{algebra!over an endofunctor}, is a pair $(A , f)$ where $A$ is an object of $\mathscr{C}$ together with a morphism $f\colon F A \to A$ in  $\mathscr{C}$, with no further assumptions. 
   An \emph{algebra homomorphism} $\eta \colon (A , f) \to (B, g)$ consists of a morphism $\eta\colon  A \to B$ such that the following diagram commutes in $\mathscr{C}$
    \[
         \begin{tikzcd}
             FA \ar[r,"F \eta"] \ar[d,"f "'] & FB \ar[d,"g"]
             \\ 
             A \ar[r,"\eta "] & B.
         \end{tikzcd}
    \]
    Let $\mathrm{Alg}_{F}{\mathscr{C}}$, or simply $\mathrm{Alg}$ if $\mathscr{C}$ and $F$ are understood,  denote the category of algebras of $F$. We denote by $\gls{AlgHom}$ the set of algebra homomorphisms $A\to B$.
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- definition-10: body_md -->
\label{def: poly endofunctor and w-type}
    Consider a category $\mathscr{C}$, objects $A, B$ of $\mathscr{C}$, and a morphism $f \colon A \to B$. The endofunctor $\gls{PolyEndo} \colon \mathscr{C} \to \mathscr{C}$ is the composition displayed below (if it exists):
    \[
         \begin{tikzcd}
          \mathscr{C}\ar{r}{-\times A}  &    \mathscr{C} / A \ar[r,"\prod_f"]  &  \mathscr{C} / B \ar[r,"\textsc{dom}"] &  \mathscr{C}.
         \end{tikzcd}
    \]
    Here, $- \times A$ denotes the functor that takes an object $X \in \mathscr{C}$ to the object $\pi_A \colon X \times A \to A$ in the slice category $\mathscr{C} / A$. The functor $\prod_f \colon \mathscr{C} / A \to \mathscr{C} / B$ denotes the right adjoint to pullback along $f$, and $\textsc{dom}$ is the functor that sends an object $X \to B$ of $\mathscr{C} / B$ to $X$.
 By \emph{polynomial endofunctor on $\mathscr{C}$} we mean any endofunctor on $\mathscr{C}$ obtained in this way.
Given a  $f \colon A \to B$, we denote by $W(f)$ the initial algebra of the endofunctor $\mathcal P_f$. A \emph{(categorical) W-type} \index{W-type} is an algebra of the form $W(f)$.
<!-- end definition-10 -->
<!-- example-13: body_md -->
Consider polynomial endofunctors on $\mathrm{Set}$. Consider two sets $A$ and $B$ and a function $f \colon A \to B$. Note that for an object $X \in \mathscr{C}$, we have
\begin{align*}
   \mathcal P_f X &\coloneqq \textsc{dom} \ \prod_f (X \times A) \\
    &\cong \sum_{b \in B} {\mathrm{Set} / B}(b , \prod_f (X \times A))\\ 
    &\cong \sum_{b \in B} {\mathrm{Set} / A}(f^{-1} b , X \times A) \\
    &\cong \sum_{b \in B} {\mathrm{Set}} (f^{-1} b , X).
\end{align*}
Letting $Fb \coloneqq f^{-1} b$, we find that $\mathcal P_f X \cong \sum_{b \in B} X^{Fb}$ (where $X^{Fb}$ denotes exponentiation, i.e., the internal hom, in $\mathrm{Set}$).  Now, we find that $\mathcal P_f$ does indeed look like a polynomial.
<!-- end example-13 -->
<!-- example-14: body_md -->
Consider the endofunctor $X \mapsto 1 + X$ on $\mathrm{Set}$. We claim that we can write this as a polynomial endofunctor. That is, we want to find an $f\colon A \to B$ such that $1 + X \cong \sum_{b \in B} X^{Fb}$. Since there are two summands in $1 + X$, we take $B$ to be the set $\{\mathtt{Zero},\mathtt{Succ}\}$. We want $X^{F(\mathtt{Zero})} \cong 1$, so we take $F(\mathtt{Zero}) \cong \emptyset$. We want $X^{F(\mathtt{Succ})} \cong X$, so we take $F(\mathtt{Succ}) \cong 1$. Thus, we take $f$ to be the inclusion $\{\mathtt{Succ}\} \to \{\mathtt{Zero},\mathtt{Succ}\}$.
<!-- end example-14 -->
<!-- example-15: body_md -->
\label{ex:lists-1}
    Given a type $\mathtt{a}$, we define the type of lists in $\mathtt{a}$ via the following specification in Haskell:
    \begin{align*}
        \mathtt{{\color{Green} data \ } {\color{BrickRed} List \ a \ } {\color{VioletRed} = \ } {\color{BrickRed} Nil\ } | {\ \color{BrickRed} Cons \ a \ (List \ a)}}.
    \end{align*}
    This has two constructors: $\mathtt{Nil} \colon 1 \to \mathtt{List \ a}$ and $\mathtt{Cons} \colon \mathtt{a} \times \mathtt{List \ a} \to \mathtt{List \ a}$, in categorical terms. This is equivalently a map $1 + \mathtt{a} \times \mathtt{List \ a} \to \mathtt{List \ a}$. That is, we want $\mathtt{List \ a}$ to be an algebra of the endofunctor $1 + \mathtt{a} \times - $.
    We consider this endofunctor on $\mathrm{Set}$. We have that:
    \begin{align*}
        1 + \mathtt{a} \times X &\cong X^0 + \mathtt{a} \times X^1 \\
        &\cong X^0 + \sum_{t \in \mathtt{a}} X^1 \\
        &\cong \sum_{t \in 1 + \mathtt{a}} X^{Ft},
    \end{align*}
    where $F \colon 1 + \mathtt{a} \to \mathrm{Set}$ sends the element of $1$ to $0$, the empty set, and any $t \in \mathtt{a}$ to $1$. Thus, this is the polynomial endofunctor associated to the inclusion $i: \mathtt{a} \hookrightarrow 1 + \mathtt{a}$; that is $\mathcal P _i \cong 1 + \mathtt{a} \times - $.
    That is, where one could say that our Haskell specification has two constructors, \texttt{Nil} and \texttt{Cons}, the W-type specification has $(1 + \mathtt{a})$-many constructors.

    We now claim that the initial algebra of this endofunctor is the set of lists with entries from $\mathtt{a}$.
    To be a bit more precise, it is $\sum_{n \in \mathbb N} \mathtt{a}^n$. This has an algebra structure: we take \texttt{Nil} to correspond to the single element of $\mathtt{a}^0$ in the disjoint union, and we take $\texttt{Cons} \colon\mathtt{a} \times \mathtt{List \ a} \to \mathtt{List \ a}$ to send $(a \in \mathtt{a}, \ell \in \mathtt a^n)$ to the element $a.\ell \in \mathtt a^{n+1}$ where $a.\ell (0) \coloneqq a$ and $a.\ell(m+1) \coloneqq \ell(m)$ for any $m \in \mathbb N$. It is initial because we can use any  structure $n + c \colon 1 + \mathtt{a} \times L \to L$ of any other algebra to ``inductively'' build a unique algebra homomorphism $u: \mathtt{List \ a} \to L$. 
    Indeed, we send the single element of the summand $a^0$ in $\mathtt{List \ a}$ to the element corresponding to $n : 1 \to L$,
    and then we inductively send an element $\texttt{Cons}(a,\ell) \in a^{n+1}$ to $c(a,u\ell)$. One can check that this is an algebra homomorphism (by construction) and is the unique such.
<!-- end example-15 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
Given any function $f\colon A \to B$ in $\mathrm{Set}$, the categorical W-type $W(f)$ exists \cite[Thm.~1]{dybjer}.
    In fact, all categorical W-types exist in any topos \cite[Prop.~3.6]{mp} with a natural numbers object.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:adamek}
    Consider a category $\mathscr{C}$ with an initial object $0$ and colimits of sequences $\omega \to \mathscr{C}$, where $\omega$ denotes the countably infinite ordinal. Consider an endofunctor $F$ that preserves these colimits. Then the colimit of the following sequence is an initial algebra of $F$:
    \[ 0 \xrightarrow{!} F0 \xrightarrow{F!} F^2 0 \to \cdots. \]
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- definition-11: body_md -->
Consider an endofunctor $F$ on a category $\mathscr{C}$. A \emph{coalgebra} of $F$,\index{coalgebra!over an endofunctor} or simply an \emph{$F$-coalgebra}, is a pair $(C, f)$ where $C$ is an object of $\mathscr{C}$ and $f\colon C \to F C$ is a morphism in $\mathscr{C}$. A \emph{coalgebra homomorphism} $h\colon (C, f) \to (D, g)$ consists of a morphism $h\colon C \to D$ in $\mathscr{C}$ such that the following diagram commutes:
    \[
         \begin{tikzcd}
             C \ar[r,"h"] \ar[d,"f "'] & D \ar[d,"g"]
             \\ 
             FC \ar[r,"F h"] & FD.
         \end{tikzcd}
    \]
    The category of coalgebras, denoted $\mathrm{coAlg}_{\mathscr{C}}{F}$ or simply $\mathrm{coAlg}$ if $\mathscr{C}$ and $F$ are understood, has coalgebras of $F$ as objects and coalgebra homomorphisms as morphisms. 
    We denote by $\gls{coAlgHom}$ the set of $F$-coalgebra homomorphisms.
<!-- end definition-11 -->
<!-- definition-12: body_md -->
Given a morphism $f\colon A \to B$ in a category $\mathscr{C}$, we denote by $M(f)$ the terminal coalgebra of $\mathcal P_f$. By \emph{(categorical) M-type} we mean any coalgebra of the form $M(f)$. \index{M-type}
<!-- end definition-12 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:lambek}
    Consider an endofunctor on a category with an initial algebra $(A, \alpha)$ and a terminal coalgebra $(C,\chi)$. Then we find the following.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \par The morphisms $\alpha$ and $\chi$ are isomorphisms.
        \par The pair $(A, \alpha^{-1})$ is a coalgebra. Dually, $(C,\chi^{-1})$ is an algebra.
        \par There is a morphism $A \to C$.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- example-16: body_md -->
\label{example: terminal coalgebra of Nat}
    \label{ex: terminal coalgebra for 1 + -}
    Consider the endofunctor $1 + \mathrm{id} \colon\mathrm{Set} \to \mathrm{Set}$. We saw above that its initial algebra is $\mathbb N$.
We claim that its terminal coalgebra is $\gls{TermiCoalgNat}$. The underlying set of ${\mathbb N_\infty}$ is $\mathbb N + \{\infty\}$. Its coalgebra structure ${\mathbb N_\infty} \to 1 + {\mathbb N_\infty}$ is given by sending $0$ to the unique element of the summand $1$ and any other $n$ to $n-1$, where $\infty - 1 \coloneqq \infty$.

    Given any other coalgebra $\chi\colon C \to 1 + C$, we let $\llbracket{c}\rrbracket$ denote the least $n$ such that $\chi^n (c)$ is the unique element of the summand $1$. One can check that this defines the only coalgebra homomorphism $\gls{TermiCoalgNatMap} \colon C \to {\mathbb N_\infty}$.
The induced map $\mathbb N \to {\mathbb N_\infty}$ from \cref{prop:lambek} is the inclusion.
<!-- end example-16 -->
<!-- example-17: body_md -->
Consider the endofunctor $1 + \mathtt{a} \times - \colon \mathrm{Set} \to \mathrm{Set}$. We saw in \cref{ex:lists-1} that its initial algebra is the set of (finite) lists with elements from $\mathtt{a}$.
We claim that the underlying set of its terminal coalgebra is the set of potentially infinite lists, often called \emph{streams}, with elements from $\mathtt{a}$, that is $\sum_{n \in {\mathbb N_\infty}} \mathtt{a}^n$.
    The coalgebra structure $\sum_{n \in {\mathbb N_\infty}} \mathtt{a}^n \to 1 + \mathtt{a} \times \sum_{n \in {\mathbb N_\infty}} \mathtt{a}^n$ is given by sending the element of the summand $\mathtt{a}^0$ to the element of the summand $1$. We send an $\ell \in \mathtt{a}^\infty$ to the pair $(\ell(0),\ell)$. For other $n$, we send an element $\ell \in \mathtt{a}^n$ to the pair $(\ell(0), \ell' )$ where $\ell'(m) \coloneqq \ell(m-1)$.

    There is a unique coalgebra homomorphism from any other coalgebra $C$ to this one of streams. Intuitively, one sees the map $\chi\colon C \to 1 + \mathtt{a} \times C$ as a partially defined function $\chi\colon C \to \mathtt{a} \times C$. For any $c \in C$, $\chi(c)$, if defined, is a pair of a `head' in $\mathtt{a}$ and `tail' in $C$. By repeatedly applying $\chi$ to any $c$ until it is not defined anymore, one can construct a stream from $c$. One can check that this is the unique coalgebra homomorphism.
Just as in the above example, the induced map from the initial algebra to the terminal coalgebra is the natural inclusion of lists into streams.
<!-- end example-17 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
Consider a category $\mathscr{C}$ with a terminal object $1$ and limits of sequences $\omega \to \mathscr{C}$, where $\omega$ denotes the countably infinite ordinal. Consider an endofunctor $F$ that preserves these limits. Then the limit of the following sequence is a terminal coalgebra of $F$:
    \[ \cdots \to F^2 1 \xrightarrow{F !} F 1 \xrightarrow{!} 1. \]
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- example-18: body_md -->
Our running example throughout this section will be $\mathrm{Set}$ with its cartesian monoidal structure, and the endofunctor $X \mapsto X + 1$.
<!-- end example-18 -->
<!-- definition-13: body_md -->
\label{definition: lax symmetric monoidal}
 That $(F, \nabla, \eta)$ is a \emph{lax symmetric monoidal endofunctor}\index{lax symmetric monoidal endofunctor} means that $F$ is an endofunctor on $\mathscr{C}$ with
 \begin{description}
     \par[{(L1)}:] a natural transformation $\nabla_{X,Y}\colon F X \otimes FY\longrightarrow F(X\otimes Y)$, for all $X,Y\in \mathscr{C}$; and
     \par[{(L2)}:] a morphism $\eta\colon \mathbb I\rightarrow F\mathbb I $ in $\mathscr{C}$;
 \end{description}
 such that $(F, \nabla, \eta)$ is associative, unital, and symmetric, in the sense that the following diagrams commute.
 \begin{description}
    \par[(Associativity):] For all objects $X,Y, Z\in \mathscr{C}$, the following diagram commutes:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep= large]
 FX \otimes FY \otimes FZ \ar{r}{\nabla_{X,Y}\otimes \mathrm{id}}\ar{d}[swap]{\mathrm{id}\otimes \nabla_{Y,Z}} & [2.5em] F(X\otimes Y) \otimes FZ \ar{d}{\nabla_{X\otimes Y, Z}}\\
 FX\otimes F(Y\otimes Z) \ar{r}{\nabla_{X, Y\otimes Z}} & F(X\otimes Y \otimes Z).
   \end{tikzcd}
   \]
   
   \par[(Unitality):] For all objects $X\in \mathscr{C}$, the following diagrams commute:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=scriptsize]
FX\ar[equals]{ddrr}\ar{r}{\cong} & [-1em] \mathbb I\otimes FX  \ar{r}{\eta\otimes \mathrm{id}} & F\mathbb I\otimes FX\ar{d}{\nabla_{\mathbb I, X}} & FX \ar{r}{\cong} \ar[equals]{ddrr} & [-1em]FX\otimes \mathbb I \ar{r}{\mathrm{id}\otimes \eta} & FX\otimes F\mathbb I \ar{d}{\nabla_{X, \mathbb I}}\\
 & & F(\mathbb I\otimes X) \ar{d}{\cong} & & & F(X\otimes \mathbb I)\ar{d}{\cong}\\
 [-1em]  & & FX & & & FX.
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\par[(Symmetry):] For all objects $X,Y\in \mathscr{C}$, the following diagram commutes
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
   FX \otimes FY \ar{r}{\nabla_{X,Y}} \ar{d}{\cong}[swap]{\tau_{FX,FY}}& F(X\otimes Y)\ar{d}{F(\tau_{X,Y})} [swap]{\cong}\\
   FY \otimes FX \ar{r}{\nabla_{Y,X}} & F(Y\otimes X),
\end{tikzcd}
\]
where $\tau_{X,Y}:X\otimes Y\rightarrow Y\otimes X$ is the symmetry natural isomorphism in $\mathscr{C}$.
\end{description}
<!-- end definition-13 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
One may also say \emph{symmetric lax monoidal} instead of lax  symmetric monoidal. 
    Notice the symmetry is not truly needed in our work but makes the statement of enrichment in \cref{thm:enriched} easier.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- example-19: body_md -->
For the endofunctor $\mathrm{id} + 1$, we define
    \begin{align*}
        \nabla_{X,Y}\colon (X+1)\times (Y+1) & \longrightarrow  (X\times Y)+1\\
        (x,y) & \longmapsto  \begin{cases}
            (x, y) & \text{if  }x\neq \mathtt{t},   y \neq \mathtt{t}\\
            \mathtt{t} & \text{otherwise.}
        \end{cases}
    \end{align*}
    for $x \in X, y \in Y, \mathtt{t} \in 1$. 
    We define $\eta \colon 1 \to 1 + 1$ to be the inclusion into the first summand.
<!-- end example-19 -->
<!-- example-20: body_md -->
The lax monoidal structure on $F$ determines an $F$-coalgebra structure on $\eta\colon \mathbb I\rightarrow  F(\mathbb I)$. 
One can check that the resulted convolution algebra $[\mathbb I, B]$ is isomorphic as an $F$-algebra to $B$.
<!-- end example-20 -->
<!-- definition-14: body_md -->
\label{definition: measuring coalgebra}
Consider $F$-algebras $(A,\alpha)$ and $(B, \beta)$, and a $F$-coalgebra $(C, \chi)$. 
We call a map $\varphi\colon C\otimes A\rightarrow B$ a \emph{measuring from $A$ to $B$}\index{measuring of algebras!over an endofunctor} if it makes the following diagram commute:
    \[
     \begin{tikzcd}
       & F(C)\otimes F(A) \ar{r}{\nabla_{C,A}} & F(C\otimes A) \ar{r}{F(\varphi)} & F(B) \ar{dd}{\beta}\\
      C\otimes F(A) \ar{ur}{\chi\otimes \mathrm{id}} \ar{dr}[swap]{\mathrm{id}\otimes \alpha} \\
      & C\otimes A \ar{rr}{\varphi} & & B.
     \end{tikzcd}
    \]
    We denote by \gls{MeasuringSet} the set of all measurings $C\otimes A\rightarrow B$.
<!-- end definition-14 -->
<!-- example-21: body_md -->
The monoidal unit $\mathbb I$ of $\mathscr{C}$ is a coalgebra via the lax symmetric monoidal structure $\eta\colon\mathbb I\rightarrow F(\mathbb I)$. Thus morphisms $A \to B$ in $\mathscr{C}$ are in bijection with morphisms $\mathbb I \otimes A \to B$ in $\mathscr{C}$, and one can check that a morphism $A \to B$ in $\mathscr{C}$ is an algebra homomorphism if and only if $\mathbb I \otimes A \to B$ is a measuring. Thus, $\mu_\mathbb I( A, B)\cong{\mathrm{Alg}}(A,B)$.
<!-- end example-21 -->
<!-- example-22: body_md -->
\label{ex: measuring for - + 1}
    Consider algebras $A$ and $B$ and a coalgebra $C$ for the endofunctor $X \mapsto 1 + X$.
    A measuring from $A$ to $B$ by $C$ is a function $f  \colon C \times A \rightarrow B$ such that the following three properties hold:
    \begin{description}
        \par[{(M1)}:] $f_c (0_A)=0_B$ for all $c \in C$;
        \par[{(M2)}:] $f_c(a+1)=0_B$ for all $\llbracket c \rrbracket=0$ and for all $a\in A$;
        \par[{(M3)}:] $f_c(a+1)=f_{c-1}(a)+1$ for $\llbracket c \rrbracket \geq 1$ and for all $a\in A$. 
    \end{description}
    Here, we write $f_c (a)$ for $f(c,a)$. Since $A$ has an algebra structure $A + 1 \to A$, it has a distinguished element, that we write above as $0_A$, and an endofunction, that we write above as $a + 1$; similarly for $B$. Since $C$ has a coalgebra structure, there is a unique map $\llbracket{-}\rrbracket : C \to {\mathbb N_\infty}$ (recalling that ${\mathbb N_\infty}$ is the terminal coalgebra from \cref{ex: terminal coalgebra for 1 + -}). The coalgebra structure map is a partial endofunction that we denote as $c - 1$ above.
<!-- end example-22 -->
<!-- definition-15: body_md -->
\label{definition: abstract partial homomorphism}
    Given algebras $(A, \alpha)$ and $(B,\beta)$ and a coalgebra $(C,\chi)$, a \emph{$C$-indexed partial homomorphism} from $A$ to $B$\index{partial homomorphism indexed over a coalgebra!over an endofunctor} is a map $\widetilde{\varphi}\colon C\rightarrow [A,B]$ in $\mathscr{C}$ such that its adjunct $\widehat{\varphi}\colon A\rightarrow [C, B]$ is an algebra homomorphism i.e., 
    fits in the following commutative diagram
    \[
        \begin{tikzcd}
          & F(C) \ar{r}{F(\widetilde{\varphi})} &[1em] F([A,B]) \ar{r}{\widetilde{\nabla}_{A,B}} & [1em] {[FA, FB]} \ar{dd}{\beta_*}\\
         C \ar{ur}{\chi} \ar{dr}[swap]{\widetilde{\varphi}} \\
         & {[A,B]} \ar{rr}{\alpha^*} & & {[FA,B]}
        \end{tikzcd}
       \]
    where $\alpha^*$ denotes precomposition by $\alpha$ and $\beta_*$ denotes postcomposition by $\beta$.
<!-- end definition-15 -->
<!-- definition-16: body_md -->
\label{definition: universal measuring}
Let $A$ and $B$ be $F$-algebras. We define the category of measurings $\mathscr{M}(A,B)$ from $A$ to $B$ to be the category whose objects are pairs $(C;\widetilde{\varphi})$ of an $F$-coalgebra $C$ and a $C$-indexed partial homomorphism $\widetilde{\varphi}\colon C\rightarrow [A, B]$ (or equivalently a measuring $\varphi\colon C \otimes A \to B$), and whose morphisms $(C;\widetilde{\varphi}) \to (D;\widetilde{\psi})$ are coalgebra homomorphisms $\gamma\colon C \to D$ such that the following diagram commutes
\[
 \begin{tikzcd}
C \ar{rr}{\gamma}\ar{dr}[swap]{\widetilde{\varphi}} & & D \ar{dl}{\widetilde{\psi}}\\
& {[A,B].}
 \end{tikzcd}
 \]
The \emph{universal measuring coalgebra from $A$ to $B$}\index{universal measuring coalgebra!over an endofunctor}, denoted $(\gls{UnivFMeasuring}, \widetilde{\mathrm{ev}})$, is the terminal object (if it exists) in $\mathscr{M}(A,B)$. 
                                                                   
This means given an $C$-indexed partial homomorphisms $\widetilde{\varphi}\colon C\rightarrow [A, B]$,  there exists a unique coalgebra homomorphism $u_\varphi\colon C\rightarrow {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}({A},{B})$ such that the following diagram commutes
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
    C \ar{r}{\widetilde{\varphi}} \ar[dashed]{d}[swap]{\exists! u_\varphi}& {[A, B]}\\
{\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,B). \ar[bend right]{ur}[swap]{\widetilde{\mathrm{ev}}}
\end{tikzcd}
\]
The construction is natural in $A$ and $B$ and defines a functor:
\[
{\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(-,-)\colon \mathrm{Alg}^\mathrm{op}\times \mathrm{Alg} \longrightarrow \mathrm{coAlg}.
\]
<!-- end definition-16 -->
<!-- example-23: body_md -->
$\mathrm{Set}$ is locally presentable and $\mathrm{id} + 1$ is accessible, as it preserves all filtered colimits (in fact all connected colimits).
<!-- end example-23 -->
<!-- example-24: body_md -->
The following endofunctors on a locally presentable, symmetric monoidal category $\mathscr{C}$ are always accessible and lax symmetric monoidal. 
    \begin{description}
           \par[$(\mathrm{id})$:] The identity endofunctor $\mathrm{id}_\mathscr{C}$ has a trivial lax symmetric monoidal structure and preserves filtered colimits.
           \par[$(A)$:] Given a commutative monoid $(A, \eta, \nabla) \in \mathscr{C}$, the constant endofunctor that sends each object to $A$ has a lax symmetric monoidal structure. Indeed, $\eta$ and $\nabla$ are exactly the structure required for this functor to be lax symmetric monoidal. This preserves filtered colimits.
           \par[$(GF)$:] Suppose that $(F, \eta_F, \nabla_F)$ and $(G, \eta_G, \nabla_G)$ are lax symmetric monoidal endofunctors on $\mathscr{C}$. Then so is the composition $GF$. The map $\eta$ is the composition $\mathbb I \xrightarrow{\eta_G} G (\mathbb I) \xrightarrow{G \eta_F} GF(\mathbb I)$. The map $\nabla$ is the composition $GF(X) \otimes GF(Y) \xrightarrow{\nabla_G} G(F(X) \otimes F(Y)) \xrightarrow{G\nabla_F} GF(X \otimes Y)$. If $F$ and $G$ both preserved filtered colimits, then so does $GF$.
           \par[$(F \otimes G)$:] Suppose that $\mathscr{C}$ is closed and that $(F, \eta_F, \nabla_F)$ and $(G, \eta_G, \nabla_G)$ are lax symmetric monoidal endofunctors on $\mathscr{C}$. Then so is $F \otimes G$, by which we mean the functor that takes $X \mapsto FX \otimes GX$. The map $\eta$ is the composition $\mathbb I \to \mathbb I \otimes \mathbb I \xrightarrow{\eta_F \otimes \eta_G} (F \otimes G)(\mathbb I)$. The map $\nabla$ is the composition $(F \otimes G)(X) \otimes (F \otimes G)(Y) \cong (FX \otimes FY) \otimes (GX \otimes GY) \xrightarrow{\nabla_F \otimes \nabla_G} (F \otimes G)  (X \otimes Y)$. If $F$ and $G$ are accessible, then so is $F \otimes G$ (because $\otimes$ preserves colimits in each variable, as $\mathscr{C}$ is closed). 
           \par[$(F + G)$:] Suppose $\mathscr{C}$ is closed and that $(F, \eta_F, \nabla_F)$ is a lax symmetric monoidal endofunctor, and consider a pair $(G, \nabla_G)$ of an endofunctor $G\colon \mathscr{C} \to \mathscr{C}$ and transformation $GX \otimes GY \to G(X \otimes Y)$ which is associative and symmetric (i.e.~a lax symmetric monoidal endofunctor but without $\eta$), and suppose that $G$ is a \emph{module} over $F$, meaning that there is a natural transformation $GX \otimes FY \to G(X \otimes Y)$ satisfying the diagrams of \cite[Def.~39]{yetter}, where the concept of module over a monoidal functor is defined. Then $F + G$ is a lax symmetric monoidal functor, where $F+ G$ takes $X$ to $FX + GX$. We set $\eta$ to be the composition $\mathbb I \xrightarrow{\eta_F} F (\mathbb I) \rightarrow F(\mathbb I) + G(\mathbb I) \cong (F + G)(\mathbb I)$. The map $\nabla$ is given by the following composition
           \begin{align*}
           \hspace{-1em}
               & (F + G)(X) \otimes (F + G)(Y)  \\
               \cong \ &(FX \otimes FY) + (FX \otimes GY) + (GX \otimes FY) + (GX \otimes GY) \\
                \xrightarrow{\langle \nabla_F , \lambda, \rho, \nabla_G \rangle} \ &F(X \otimes Y) + G(X \otimes Y) 
                \\ \cong \ &(F+G)(X \otimes Y).
           \end{align*} 
           If $F$ and $G$ preserve filtered colimits, then so does $F + G$.
       \par[$(\mathrm{id}^A)$:] Suppose that $\mathscr{C}$ is cartesian (so we denote it $(\mathscr{C},1 ,\times)$). Consider an exponentiable object $A$ of $\mathscr{C}$, meaning that the functor $\mathrm{id} \times A$ has a right adjoint, denoted $\mathrm{id}^A$. This has a lax symmetric monoidal structure. We let $1 \to 1^A$ and $X^A \times Y^A \to (X \times Y)^A$ be the isomorphisms we get from the fact that $-^A$, as a right adjoint, preserves limits. It is accessible as a right adjoint.
       \par[($W$-types):] Consider the cartesian monoidal structure on $\mathrm{Set}$. Consider a commutative monoid $C \in \mathrm{Set}$, which can be considered as a commutative monoidal discrete category, and a function $f\colon A \to C$ such that the preimage functor $f^{-1}\colon C \to \mathrm{Set}$ has an oplax symmetric monoidal structure. Then the polynomial endofunctor (\cref{def: poly endofunctor and w-type}) $\mathcal P_f \colon \mathrm{Set} \to \mathrm{Set}$ has a lax symmetric monoidal structure. The elements of $\mathcal P_f X$ are pairs $(c \in C, g \colon f^{-1} c \to X)$.  The natural transformation $\nabla_{X,Y} \colon \mathcal P_f X \times \mathcal P_f Y \to \mathcal P_f(X \times Y)$ takes a pair $((c, g \colon f^{-1} c \to X), (d, h \colon f^{-1} d \to X))$ to $(cd, (g \times h) \circ \Lambda_{c,d}\colon f^{-1} (cd) \to X \times Y)$ where $\Lambda_{c,d}\colon f^{-1} (cd) \to f^{-1} c \times f^{-1}d$ is part of the oplax monoidal structure of $f^{-1}$. The natural transformation $\varepsilon\colon 1 \to \mathcal P_f 1 \cong C$ is the unit of the monoidal structure on $C$. This polynomial endofunctor is accessible since it is the composition of left and right adjoints.
       \par[(Discrete equational systems):] Suppose that the monoidal structure on $\mathscr{C}$ is cocartesian, so we denote it by $(\mathscr{C},0, +)$, and suppose also that $\mathscr{C}$ also has binary products that preserve filtered colimits in each variable. Consider a \emph{discrete equational system} \cite{leinster} on $\mathscr{C}$, that is, a pair $(A,M)$ where $A$ is a set and $M$ is an object of $\mathscr{C}^{A \times A}$. The functor category $\mathscr{C}^A$ inherits a cocartesian monoidal structure $(\mathscr{C}^A ,0, +)$ pointwise. Define an endofunctor $M \otimes - \colon \mathscr{C}^A \to \mathscr{C}^A$ by setting
       \[ (M \otimes X)_a \coloneqq\sum_{b \in A} M_{b,a} \times X_b. \]
       This is lax symmetric monoidal. The morphisms $\eta\colon 0 \to M \otimes 0$ and $\nabla\colon M \otimes (X + Y) \to M \otimes X + M \otimes Y$ are induced by the universal properties of $0$ and $+$. It is also accessible since the coproducts and binary products preserve filtered colimits.
   \end{description}
<!-- end example-24 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{theorem: equalizer formula for universal measuring}
Suppose that $\mathscr{C}$ is a symmetric monoidal closed category that is locally presentable, and that $F\colon \mathscr{C}\rightarrow \mathscr{C}$ is a symmetric lax monoidal, accessible endofunctor.
Given $F$-algebras $A$ and $B$, then the universal measuring coalgebra $({\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,B), \widetilde{\mathrm{ev}})$ exists and is determined as the following equalizer diagram in ${\mathrm{coAlg}}$:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
   {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,B) \ar[dashed]{r}{\overline{\mathrm{ev}}} & \mathrm{Cof}\big( [A,B]\big) \ar[shift left]{r}{\Phi} \ar[shift right]{r}[swap]{\Psi} & \mathrm{Cof}\big( [FA, B]\big).
\end{tikzcd}
\]
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Since every $C$-indexed partial homomorphism $\widetilde{\varphi}\colon C\rightarrow [A, B]$ is equivalent to a coalgebra homomorphism $C\rightarrow \mathrm{Cof}([A,B])$ that coequalizes the parallel morphisms described above, we see that the category $\mathscr{M}(A,B)$ of measurings from $A$ to $B$ is equivalent to the category of cones over the aforementioned parallel morphisms.
Thus they have equivalent terminal objects ${\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,B)$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- definition-17: body_md -->
\label{ex: dual}
    Suppose that $\mathscr{C}$ is a symmetric monoidal closed category that is locally presentable, and that $F\colon \mathscr{C}\rightarrow \mathscr{C}$ is a symmetric lax monoidal, accessible endofunctor.
    The category ${\mathrm{Alg}}$ has an initial object which we denote by $N$.
    
    Let $(-)^*\colon{\mathrm{coAlg}}^\mathrm{op}\rightarrow {\mathrm{Alg}}$ denote the functor $[-,N]$, and call $C^*$ the \emph{dual algebra of $C$} for any coalgebra $C$.

    Let $(-)^\circ\colon{\mathrm{Alg}}^\mathrm{op}\rightarrow {\mathrm{coAlg}}$ denote the functor ${\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(-,N)$, and call $A^\circ$ the \emph{dual coalgebra of $A$} for any algebra $A$.
    
    These functors form a dual adjunction in the sense that 
we obtain natural identifications for all $C\in \mathrm{coAlg}$ and $A\in \mathrm{Alg}$:
    \[
    {\mathrm{Alg}}(A, C^*)\cong {\mathrm{coAlg}}(C, A^\circ).
    \]
<!-- end definition-17 -->
<!-- definition-18: body_md -->
Let $C$ be an $F$-coalgebra and $A$ an $F$-algebra. 
We define $\mathscr{M}_C(A)$ to be the category whose objects consist of pairs $(B, \varphi)$ where $B$ is an $F$-algebra, and $\varphi\colon C\otimes A\rightarrow B$ is a $C$-measuring from $A$ to $B$.
A morphism $(B_1, \varphi)\rightarrow (B_2, \psi)$ in $\mathscr{M}_C(A)$ consists of an algebra homomorphism $B_1\rightarrow B_2$ fitting in the commutative diagram in $\mathscr{C}$:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
    & C\otimes A \ar{dl}[swap]{\varphi} \ar{dr}{\psi}\\
    B_1 \ar{rr} & & B_2.
\end{tikzcd}
\]
If it exists, we denote by $(C\triangleright A, u)$ the initial object of $\mathscr{M}_C(A)$. The $F$-algebra $\gls{MeasTens}$ is called the \emph{measuring tensor of $C$ with $A$},\index{measuring tensor!over an endofunctor} and its measuring $u\colon C\otimes A\rightarrow C\triangleright A$ is the universal $C$-measuring from $A$.
In other words, given any $C$-measuring $\varphi\colon C\otimes A\rightarrow B$, there exists a unique algebra homomorphism $!\colon C\triangleright A\rightarrow B$ such that the following diagram commutes in $\mathscr{C}$:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
    C\otimes A \ar{r}{\varphi} \ar{d}[swap]{u} & B\\
    C\triangleright A. \ar[dashed]{ur}[swap]{!}
\end{tikzcd}
\]
The construction is natural in $C$ and $A$ and thus determines a functor
\[
-\triangleright -\colon \mathrm{coAlg}\times  \mathrm{Alg} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Alg}.
\]
<!-- end definition-18 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{thm: copower}
Suppose that $\mathscr{C}$ symmetric monoidal closed category that is locally presentable, and that $F\colon \mathscr{C}\rightarrow \mathscr{C}$ is an accessible endofunctor.
Consider an $F$-coalgebra $C$ and an $F$-algebra $A$.
The measuring tensor $(C\triangleright A, u)$ exists and is determined as the following coequalizer in ${\mathrm{Alg}}$:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
   \mathrm{Fr}(C\otimes FA)\ar[shift left]{r}{\Phi} \ar[shift right]{r}[swap]{\Psi} & \mathrm{Fr}(C\otimes A) \ar[dashed]{r}{u'} & C\triangleright A.
\end{tikzcd}
\]
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
\label{remark: universal measuring as an adjoint}
The convolution algebra also provides an alternative characterization of the algebra $C\triangleright A$ and coalgebra ${\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,B)$.
As limits in ${\mathrm{Alg}}$ and colimits in ${\mathrm{coAlg}}$ are determined in $\mathscr{C}$ \cite{varieties} and the internal hom $[-,-]\colon\mathscr{C}^\mathrm{op}\times \mathscr{C}\rightarrow \mathscr{C}$ preserves limits, the functor $[-,-]\colon{\mathrm{coAlg}}^\mathrm{op}\times {\mathrm{Alg}}\rightarrow {\mathrm{Alg}}$ also preserves limits. 
Moreover, fixing a coalgebra $C$, the induced functor $[C, -]\colon{\mathrm{Alg}}\rightarrow {\mathrm{Alg}}$ is accessible since filtered colimits in ${\mathrm{Alg}}$ are computed in $\mathscr{C}$ (see \cite[5.6]{varieties}). 
Therefore, by the adjoint functor theorem \cite[1.66]{presentable}, the functor $[C,-]$ is a right adjoint. Its left adjoint is precisely $C\triangleright -\colon{\mathrm{Alg}}\rightarrow {\mathrm{Alg}}$. Indeed, for any algebras $A$ and $B$, we obtain the following bijection, natural in $C,A,B$.
\[
{\mathrm{Alg}} \big( C\triangleright A, B\big) \cong {\mathrm{Alg}} \big(A, [C,B]\big).
\]
Notice we can also determine the universal measuring coalgebra by using the adjoint functors.
Fixing now an algebra $B$, the opposite functor $[-,B]^\mathrm{op}\colon{\mathrm{coAlg}}\rightarrow {\mathrm{Alg}}^\mathrm{op}$ preserves colimits, where the domain is locally presentable and the codomain is essentially locally small. By the adjoint functor theorem \cite[1.66]{presentable}, this functor is a left adjoint. 
Its right adjoint is precisely the functor ${\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(-, B)\colon{\mathrm{Alg}}^\mathrm{op}\rightarrow {\mathrm{coAlg}}$. Indeed, for any algebra $A$ and $B$ and any coalgebra $C$, we have the following bijection, natural in $C,A,B$:
\begin{align*}
{\mathrm{coAlg}}\big( C, {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,B) \big) \cong {\mathrm{Alg}} \big( A, [C,B]\big).
\end{align*}
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- definition-19: body_md -->
Say that an algebra $A$ is \emph{preinitial} \index{preinitial algebra} if the universal map $I \to A$ from the initial algebra $I$ is an epimorphism (in ${\mathrm{Alg}}$). Dually, a coalgebra $C$ is \emph{subterminal} \index{subterminal coalgebra} if the universal map $C \to T$ to the terminal coalgebra $C$ is a monomorphism (in ${\mathrm{coAlg}}$).
<!-- end definition-19 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{lem: quotient algebras}
        Consider a category $\mathscr{C}$, an endofunctor $F\colon \mathscr{C} \to \mathscr{C}$, and an algebra $(A,\alpha)$ of $F$.
        \begin{enumerate}
            \par Given a quotient object $Q$ of $A$ for which $\alpha$ restricts to a map $\alpha_Q \colon FQ \to Q$, then the pair $(Q, \alpha_Q)$ is a quotient object of $(A, \alpha)$.
            \par If the forgetful functor $\mathrm{Alg} \to \mathscr{C}$ preserves epimorphisms, then for every quotient object $(Q, \alpha_Q)$ of $(A, \alpha)$, $Q$ is a quotient object of $A$.
        \end{enumerate}
        Thus, if the forgetful functor preserves epimorphisms, it induces an isomorphism between the poset of quotient algebras of $(A,\alpha_A)$ and the poset of quotient objects $Q$ of $A$ for which $\alpha$ restricts to a morphism $\alpha_Q \colon FQ \to Q$.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
For (1), asking that $\alpha$ restricts to a map $\alpha_Q$ is exactly asking that $(Q, \alpha_Q)$ is an algebra of $F$ and that the quotient map constitutes a total algebra homomorphism $q\colon (A, \alpha) \to (Q, \alpha_Q)$. 
        Since the forgetful functor $\mathrm{Alg} \to \mathscr{C}$ is faithful, it reflects epimorphisms. The second statement (2) is immediate.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- example-25: body_md -->
\label{ex: quotient algebras for id + 1}
        Consider the endofunctor $\mathrm{id} + 1$ on $\mathrm{Set}$. Since the forgetful functor $\mathrm{Alg} \to \mathscr{C}$ preserves epimorphisms, there is an isomorphism between the poset of quotient algebras of an algebra $(A,\alpha)$ and the poset of quotient sets $Q$ of $A$ for which $\alpha$ restricts to a morphism $\alpha_Q \colon FQ \to Q$.
    Thus, nontrivial preinitial algebras include those of the form
${\mathbb {n}} \coloneqq (\{0,1,...,n\}, \alpha_{\mathbb {n}})$ for any $n \in \mathbb N$ where $\alpha_{\mathbb {n}}$ is the algebra structure that $\{0,1,...,n\}$ inherits as the quotient of $\mathbb N$ in $\mathrm{Set}$ that identifies all $m \geq n$.
<!-- end example-25 -->
<!-- definition-20: body_md -->
Consider a category $\mathscr{C}$ with a terminal object $1$, an endofunctor $F\colon \mathscr{C} \to \mathscr{C}$, and suppose that the category of coalgebras of $F$ has a terminal coalgebra $T$.
        \begin{itemize}
            \par  Call a point $1 \to T$ an \emph{index}. For any index $n$, let ${\mathrm{coAlg}}^n$ denote the category whose objects are pairs $((X, \chi_X), x)$ where $(X, \chi_X)$ is a coalgebra and $x\colon 1 \to X$ such that $\llbracket{x}\rrbracket = n$, using the notation of \cref{example: terminal coalgebra of Nat}.
            \par Say that a coalgebra is \emph{freely generated by a point of index $n$} if it is an initial object in ${\mathrm{coAlg}}^n$. Say that a coalgebra is \emph{generated by a point of index $n$} if it is the vertex of a cone on the identity endofunctor on ${\mathrm{coAlg}}^n$.
        \end{itemize}
<!-- end definition-20 -->
<!-- definition-21: body_md -->
Say that $F \colon\mathscr{C} \to \mathscr{C} $ is \emph{well-equipped} \index{well-equipped endofunctor} if $\mathscr{C}$ is well-pointed and for every index $n$, there is a coalgebra generated by a point of index $n$.
<!-- end definition-21 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:char-sub}
        Consider a category $\mathscr{C}$, an endofunctor $F$, and a coalgebra $(C, \chi)$.
        \begin{enumerate}
            \par Given a subobject $S$ of $C$ for which $\chi$ restricts to a morphism $\chi_S\colon S \to FS$, the pair $(S, \chi_S)$ is a subobject of $(C, \chi)$.
            \par If $F$ is well-equipped, then for every subcoalgebra $(S, \chi_S)$ of $(C, \chi)$, we have that $S$ is a subobject of $C$.
        \end{enumerate}
        Thus, if $F$ is well-equipped, there is an isomorphism between the poset of subobjects of $(C, \chi_C)$ and the poset of subobjects of $C$ for which $\chi_C$ restricts to a morphism $\chi_S\colon FS \to S$.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
For (1), consider $\iota \colon S \rightarrowtail C$. Asking that $\chi$ restricts to a morphism $\chi_S$ means exactly that $\iota$ constitutes a total algebra homomorphism $\iota \colon (S, \chi_C) \to (C, \chi)$. This is a monomorphism since the forgetful functor $U\colon \mathrm{Alg} \to \mathscr{C}$ is faithful and thus reflects monomorphisms.

    For (2), consider a monomorphism $\iota\colon(S, \chi_S) \rightarrowtail (C, \chi)$. In order to show that $\iota \colon S \to C$ is also a monomorphism, consider two points $x, y\colon1 \to S$ in $\mathscr{C}$ such that $\iota x = \iota y$. Since $\mathscr{C}$ is assumed to be well-pointed, it suffices to show that $x = y$. Note that $\llbracket{x}\rrbracket = \llbracket{\iota x}\rrbracket = \llbracket{\iota y}\rrbracket =  \llbracket{y}\rrbracket$, and let $((I, \chi_I), \top_n)$ denote a coalgebra generated by a point of this index. Then we get two maps $\overline x, \overline y\colon(I, \chi_I) \to (S, \chi_S)$ and a map $\overline{\iota x} = \overline{\iota y} \colon (I, \chi_I) \to (C, \chi)$ such that $\iota \overline x = \overline{\iota x} = \overline{\iota y} = \iota \overline y$. Since $\iota$ is a monomorphism, $\overline x = \overline y$, but then $x = \overline x \top_n = \overline y \top_n = y\colon * \to \mathscr{C}$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- example-26: body_md -->
\label{ex: subcoalgebras for id + 1}
        Consider the endofunctor $\mathrm{id} + 1$ on $\mathrm{Set}$. The nontrivial subsets of ${\mathbb N_\infty}$ that are closed under the coalgebra morphism are $\{0,1,...,n\}$, $\{\infty\}$, $\mathbb N$ (and unions of these); let $\gls{subterm1}, \mathbb I, \gls{subterm2}$ denote the corresponding subterminal coalgebras. By the preceding proposition, these are the generating sub-coalgebras of ${\mathbb N_\infty}$.
        The indices are the elements of ${\mathbb N_\infty}$. Each coalgebra ${\mathbb {n}^\circ}$ is freely generated by a point of index $n$ for finite $n$, and $\mathbb I$ is freely generated by a point of index $\infty$.
<!-- end example-26 -->
<!-- example-27: body_md -->
\label{ex: partial induction}
    Consider algebras $A$ and $B$ of the endofunctor $1 + \mathrm{id}$ on $\mathrm{Set}$.
    Suppose that $A$ is preinitial, so that in particular every element of $A$ is of the form $0_A$ or $a + 1$.
    If we want to construct an algebra homomorphism $f\colon A \to B$, we can proceed by induction. First, we send $0_A \mapsto 0_B$. Next, we can try to send $1_A \mapsto 1_B$ (where $-_A$ denotes the algebra morphism $\mathbb N \to A$). Note that this only works if $1_A$ is different from $0_A$ or if $0_B = 1_B$. If this works, we can try to continue inductively, sending $n_A \mapsto n_B$. If this procedure succeeds, then we will have constructed an algebra homomorphism $f\colon A \to B$ by induction.
    
    We can turn this construction into a sequence of functions that we define in the following way.
    \begin{description}
        \par[{Initial step (P1)}:] Define $f_0\colon A\rightarrow B$ by $f_0(a)\coloneqq 0_B$ for all $a\in A$. 
        \par[{Inductive step}:] Define $f_{c+1} \colon A\rightarrow B$ by:
        \begin{description}
            \par[{(P2)}:] $f_{c+1}(0_A)\coloneqq 0_B$;
            \par[{(P3)}:] $f_{c+1}(a+1)\coloneqq f_{c}(a)+1$.
        \end{description}
    \end{description}
    If we have defined $f_c$ for all $c \in \mathbb N$, then we will say that we have defined an \emph{$\infty$-partial homomorphism}. Note that in this case, one can then form a total algebra homomorphism which we will denote $f_\infty$.
Otherwise, if we have only defined $f_c$ for all $c \in \{0, ..., n\}$, we will say that we have defined an \emph{$n$-partial homomorphism}.
    Now compare this induction with the definition of measuring (\cref{ex: measuring for - + 1}).
    There is a measuring from $A$ to $B$ by ${\mathbb {n}^\circ}$ if the induction above creates an $n$-partial homomorphism, and in this case the functions of the form $f_c$ constructed are the same as those specified in \cref{ex: measuring for - + 1}.

    If we denote $\mathrm{Alg}_n(A,B)\coloneqq \mu_{\mathbb{n}^\circ}(A,B)\cong \mathrm{coAlg}(\mathbb{n}^\circ, {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,B))$ the set of all $\mathbb{n}^\circ$-measurings from $A$ to $B$, the natural inclusions $\mathbb{n}^\circ\hookrightarrow (\mathbb{n}+1)^\circ$ are homomorphisms of coalgebras, so after applying the functor $\mathrm{coAlg}(-, {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,B))\colon \mathrm{coAlg}^\mathrm{op}\rightarrow \mathrm{Set}$, we obtain a tower
     \[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=small]
    \mathrm{Alg}_\infty(A,B)\ar{r} & \cdots \ar{r} &
    \mathrm{Alg}_2(A,B) \ar{r}&
    \mathrm{Alg}_1(A,B) \ar{r}&
    \mathrm{Alg}_0(A,B),
\end{tikzcd}    
\] 
whose limit is $\mathrm{Alg}_\infty(A,B)\coloneqq \mathrm{coAlg}(\mathbb N^c, \mathrm{Alg}(A,B))$ as the right adjoint functor $\mathrm{coAlg}(-, {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,B))$ sends colimit in $\mathrm{coAlg}$ to a limit in $\mathrm{Set}$,  and the colimit the coalgebra homomorphisms $\mathbb{n}^{\circ}\hookrightarrow (\mathbb{n}+1)^\circ$ is precisely the coalgebra $\mathbb N^c$.
Our construction above of $f_\infty$ precisely builds, layer by layer in the tower, an element of $\mathrm{Alg}_\infty(A,B)$.
    
    There is a measuring by $\mathbb N^c$ if the induction never fails, and again the functions $f_c$ from the induction above and \cref{ex: measuring for - + 1} coincide. Now, note that exhibiting a measuring by ${\mathbb N_\infty}$ amounts to exhibiting a measuring by $\mathbb N^c$ together with a total algebra homomorphism $f_\infty$. For such an $A$, then, exhibiting a measuring by $\mathbb N^c$ is (logically) equivalent to exhibiting one by ${\mathbb N_\infty}$.
<!-- end example-27 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:subobject}
    Consider two algebras $A,B$ such that $A$ is preinitial. Then ${\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,B)$ is a subterminal coalgebra, and it is the maximum subterminal coalgebra $C$ such that ${\mathrm{Alg}}(A, [C,B])$ is nonempty.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
We first claim that ${\mathrm{Alg}}(A, [C,B])$ is empty or a singleton for any coalgebra $C$.
    Since $!_A\colon \mathbb N \to A$ is an epimorphism, the function
    \[{\mathrm{Alg}}(A, [C,B]) \xrightarrow{!^*_A}  {\mathrm{Alg}}(\mathbb N, [C,B]) \]
    is an injection, and since $\mathbb N$ is initial, ${\mathrm{Alg}}(\mathbb N, [C,B]) \cong *$.
    Thus, ${\mathrm{Alg}}(A, [C,B])$ is a singleton, in the case where the only map $\mathbb N \to [C,B]$ factors through $A$, and otherwise is empty.

    We now claim that the canonical map $\llbracket{-}\rrbracket\colon{\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,B) \to {\mathbb N_\infty}$ is a monomorphism. Suppose there are maps $a,b\colon C \to {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,B)$ from a coalgebra $C$ such that $\llbracket{a}\rrbracket = \llbracket{b}\rrbracket$. Recall that the coalgebra ${\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,B)$ is defined by the following universal property for any coalgebra $C$
    \[ {\mathrm{coAlg}}(C,{\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,B)) \cong {\mathrm{Alg}}(A, [C,B]).\]
    Thus, ${\mathrm{coAlg}}(C,{\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,B))$ is a singleton, so $a = b$, and $\llbracket{-}\rrbracket$ is monic.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- example-28: body_md -->
\label{ex:universal measuring for preinitial}
    Again, consider algebras $A$ and $B$ of the endofunctor $1 + \mathrm{id}$ on $\mathrm{Set}$ where $A$ is preinitial.
    In this case, the universal measuring is a subterminal coalgebra by the above. If the induction of \cref{ex: partial induction} succeeds in constructing $f_i$ for $i \leq n$ but fails to construct $f_{n+1}$, then the maximum subterminal coalgebra that measures $A \to B$ is ${\mathbb {n}^\circ}$, so this is the universal measuring. And if the induction of \cref{ex: partial induction} creates an $\infty$-partial homomorphism, i.e., a total homomorphism, then the maximum subterminal coalgebra that measures $A$ to $B$ is ${\mathbb N_\infty}$ itself, so this is the universal measuring.
    We will also show this fact more directly (i.e., without reference to \cref{lem:subobject}) below.
<!-- end example-28 -->
<!-- example-29: body_md -->
\label{ex: compute partial alg hom}
We compute ${\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}({\mathbb {n}},B)$ for any algebra $B$ of $1 + \mathrm{id}$ using \cref{eq: universal prop of measuring}.
We first observe the following for any algebra $Z$:
\[ {\mathrm{Alg}}({\mathbb {n}} , Z) \cong 
\begin{cases} 
    * & \text{if } n_{Z} = (n+1)_{Z} \\ \emptyset & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\] 
Since we are considering $Z\coloneqq [C,B]$, we need to understand when $n_{[C,B]} = (n+1)_{[C,B]}$. By definition, $0_{[C,A]}$ is the constant function at $0_A$. Then $1_{[C,A]}$ is the function that takes every $c \in C$ of index $0$ to $0_B$, and every other $c \in C$ to $1_B$. Inductively, we can show that $n_{[C,B]}(c) = \min(\llbracket c \rrbracket , n)_{B}$.
Thus, $n_{[C,B]} = (n+1)_{[C,B]}$ means that $\min(\llbracket c \rrbracket , n)_{B} = \min(\llbracket c \rrbracket , n + 1)_{B}$ for all $c \in C$, and this holds if and only if $\llbracket c \rrbracket \leq n$ for all $c \in C$ or $n_B = (n+1)_B$. Now we have the following:
\begin{align}\label{eq: conv alg calc}
    {\mathrm{coAlg}}(C ,  {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}({\mathbb {n}},B)) \cong {\mathrm{Alg}}({\mathbb {n}} , [C,B]) \cong
\begin{cases} 
    * & \text{if } \llbracket c \rrbracket \leq n \text{ for all } c \in C \\ 
    * & \text{if } n_B = (n+1)_B \\
    \emptyset & \text{otherwise.} 
\end{cases}
\end{align}
In the case that $n_B = (n+1)_B$, we find that ${\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}({\mathbb {n}},B)$ has the universal property of the terminal object, ${\mathbb N_\infty}$.
Now suppose that $n_B \neq (n+1)_B$. Since ${\mathrm{coAlg}}(C, {\mathbb {n}^\circ}) = *$ if and only if $\llbracket c \rrbracket \leq n$ for all $c \in C$, ${\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}({\mathbb {n}},B)$ has the universal property of ${\mathbb {n}^\circ}$. 

Now we have calculated the following 
\[ {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}({\mathbb {n}},B) = \begin{cases}
    {\mathbb N_\infty} \text{ if } n_B = (n+1)_B \\
    {\mathbb {n}^\circ} \text{ otherwise.}
\end{cases} \]
This aligns with our expectations, since there is a total homomorphism ${\mathbb {n}} \to B$ if $n_B = (n+1)_B$ but there is only an $n$-partial homomorphism ${\mathbb {n}} \to B$ otherwise.
Finally, note that taking $B \coloneqq\mathbb N$, we have calculated ${\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}({\mathbb {n}},\mathbb N)$, the \emph{dual} (\cref{ex: dual}) of ${\mathbb {n}}$, to be ${\mathbb {n}^\circ}$.
<!-- end example-29 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:sym-mon}
    Let $\mathscr{C}$ be a (symmetric) monoidal category.
    Let $F\colon \mathscr{C}\rightarrow \mathscr{C}$ be a lax (symmetric) monoidal functor.
    Then the category $\mathrm{coAlg}$ has a (symmetric) monoidal structure for which the forgetful functor $\mathrm{coAlg}\rightarrow \mathscr{C}$ is strong (symmetric) monoidal.
    Moreover, if $\mathscr{C}$ is locally presentable and closed, and $F$ is accessible, then $\mathrm{coAlg}$ is also closed, with internal hom denoted $\underline{\mathrm{coAlg}}(-,-)$.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Suppose $(C, \chi_C)$ and $(D, \chi_D)$ are coalgebras. Then $C\otimes D$ has the following coalgebra structure:
    \[
\begin{tikzcd}
{C \otimes D} \ar{r}{\chi_C \otimes \chi_D} & [1em] {F(C) \otimes F(D)} \ar{r}{\nabla_{C,D}} & {F(C\otimes D).}
\end{tikzcd}
\]
The morphism $\eta\colon \mathbb I\rightarrow F(\mathbb I)$ provides the coalgebraic structure on $\mathbb I$.

To see that $({\mathrm{coAlg}}, \otimes, (\mathbb I, \eta))$ is a symmetric monoidal category, we first need to check that $(C, \chi_C)\otimes (\mathbb I, \eta)\cong (C, \chi_C)$. On objects, we have $C\otimes \mathbb I\cong C$ as $\mathbb I$ is a monoidal unit. The coalgebraic structures correspond as we have the following commutative diagram by unitality of $(F, \nabla, \eta)$:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
   C \ar{r}{\cong}\ar{d}[swap]{\chi} & C\otimes \mathbb I \ar{dr}{\chi\otimes \eta} \\
   F(C) \ar[bend right=2em, equals]{rrrr} \ar{r}{\cong} & F(C)\otimes \mathbb I \ar{r}[swap]{\mathrm{id}\otimes \eta}& F(C)\otimes F(\mathbb I) \ar{r}{\nabla} & F(C\otimes \mathbb I)\ar{r}{\cong}  & F(C).
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Similarly, we have a natural isomorphism $ (\mathbb I, \eta)\otimes (C, \chi_C)\cong (C, \chi_C)$ from the identification $\mathbb I\otimes C\cong C$. 
Moreover, we also have the following natural isomorphism
\[
((C, \chi)\otimes (C', \chi')) \otimes (C'', \chi'') \cong (C, \chi)\otimes ((C', \chi') \otimes (C'', \chi'')),
\]
lifted from $(C\otimes C')\otimes C''\cong C\otimes (C'\otimes C'')$.
Lastly, the symmetry $C\otimes C'\cong C'\otimes C$ lifts to ${\mathrm{coAlg}}$. Therefore as $\mathscr{C}$ is symmetric monoidal, the above natural identifications assemble to a symmetric monoidal structure on ${\mathrm{coAlg}}$ as the pentagon, triangle, hexagon and symmetric identities remain valid in ${\mathrm{coAlg}}$.

Suppose now that $\mathscr{C}$ is locally presentable and closed, and $F$ is accessible. Then for all objects $X\in \mathscr{C}$, we have that $X\otimes -\colon \mathscr{C}\rightarrow \mathscr{C}$ is a left adjoint functor,  with right adjoint given by its the internal hom $[X, -]\colon \mathscr{C}\rightarrow \mathscr{C}$. 
Since $\mathrm{coAlg}$ is also locally presentable and colimits are computed in $\mathscr{C}$, we get that for all $C\in \mathrm{coAlg}$, the induced functor $C\otimes -\colon \mathrm{coAlg}\rightarrow \mathrm{coAlg}$ also preserves all colimits and thus must be a left adjoint as $\mathrm{coAlg}$ is locally presentable. 
We denote by $\underline{\mathrm{coAlg}}(C,-)\colon \mathrm{coAlg}\rightarrow \mathrm{coAlg}$ its right adjoint. The construction is natural in $C$ and thus defines the desired closed structure on $\mathrm{coAlg}$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{thm:enriched}
Suppose that $\mathscr{C}$ is a locally presentable, symmetric monoidal closed category. Let $F\colon \mathscr{C} \to \mathscr{C} $ be an accessible lax symmetric monoidal endofunctor.
Then the category ${\mathrm{Alg}}$ is enriched, tensored, and cotensored over the closed symmetric monoidal category ${\mathrm{coAlg}}$ respectively via
\[
{\mathrm{Alg}}^\mathrm{op} \times {\mathrm{Alg}}\xrightarrow{{\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(-,-)} {\mathrm{coAlg}}, \quad {\mathrm{coAlg}}\times {\mathrm{Alg}} \xrightarrow{-\triangleright-} {\mathrm{Alg}}, \quad {\mathrm{coAlg}}^\mathrm{op}\times {\mathrm{Alg}}\xrightarrow{[-,-]} {\mathrm{Alg}}.
\]
In other words, for any coalgebra $C$, and algebras $A$ and $B$, we obtain the natural identifications in $\mathrm{coAlg}$:
\[
  \underline{\mathrm{coAlg}}(C, {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,B))\cong {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(C \triangleright A, B) \cong {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A, [C, B]).  
\]
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
The convolution algebra functor $[-,-]\colon{\mathrm{coAlg}}^\mathrm{op}\times {\mathrm{Alg}}\rightarrow {\mathrm{Alg}}$ presents ${\mathrm{Alg}}$ as a right module over ${\mathrm{coAlg}}^\mathrm{op}$. 
    Thus ${\mathrm{Alg}}^\mathrm{op}$ is a left module over ${\mathrm{coAlg}}$ via \[[-,-]^\mathrm{op}\colon {\mathrm{coAlg}}\times {\mathrm{Alg}}^\mathrm{op} \rightarrow {\mathrm{Alg}}^\mathrm{op}.\] 
    Moreover, for any $A\in {\mathrm{Alg}}$, the functor $[-,B]^\mathrm{op}\colon{\mathrm{coAlg}}\rightarrow {\mathrm{Alg}}^\mathrm{op}$ 
    has a right adjoint ${\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(-, B)\colon{\mathrm{Alg}}^\mathrm{op}\rightarrow {\mathrm{coAlg}}$ as shown in \cref{remark: universal measuring as an adjoint}.
    Thus, by \cite[3.1]{hylandetal}, the category ${\mathrm{Alg}}^\mathrm{op}$ is enriched over ${\mathrm{coAlg}}$ with tensor $[-,-]^\mathrm{op}$. 
    Therefore ${\mathrm{Alg}}$ is enriched over ${\mathrm{coAlg}}$ with power $[-,-]$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
While $\mathrm{Alg}$ is enriched in $\mathrm{coAlg}$, we cannot dualize our arguments to show that $\mathrm{coAlg}$ is enriched in $\mathrm{Alg}$.
    This is because if $\mathscr{C}$ is locally presentable, then $\mathscr{C}^\mathrm{op}$ is generally not locally presentable \cite[1.64]{presentable}. 
    Instead, just as in \cref{remark: coalgebras measurings and universal internal hom}, the internal hom in $\mathrm{coAlg}$ provides that  $\mathrm{coAlg}$ is enriched, tensored, and cotensored over itself. Given $F$-coalgebras $(C, \chi)$, $(C_1, \chi_1)$ and $(C_2, \chi_2)$, we say a morphism $\widetilde{\varphi}\colon C\rightarrow [C_1, C_2]$ is a\emph{ $C$-indexed partial homomorphism} if its adjunct $\varphi\colon C\otimes C_1\rightarrow C_2$ is a homomorphism of coalgebras (which can be renamed as a \emph{$C$-measuring from $C_1$ to $C_2$}).
    In other words, this means we obtain the commutative diagram in $\mathscr{C}$
    \[
        \begin{tikzcd}
          & F(C) \ar{r}{F(\widetilde{\varphi})} &[1em] F([C_1,C_2]) \ar{r}{\widetilde{\nabla}_{C_1,C_2}} & [1em] {[FC_1, FC_2]} \ar{dd}{\chi_1^*}\\
         C \ar{ur}{\chi} \ar{dr}[swap]{\widetilde{\varphi}} \\
         & {[C_1,C_2]} \ar{rr}{(\chi_2)_*} & & {[C_1,FC_2]}.
        \end{tikzcd}
       \]
    Then the internal hom $\underline{\mathrm{coAlg}}(C_1, C_2)$ can be viewed as the universal measuring coalgebra in the sense that given any $C$-indexed partial homomorphism $\widetilde{\varphi}\colon C\rightarrow [C_1, C_2]$ (or equivalently a measuring $\varphi\colon C\otimes C_1\rightarrow C_2$), there exists a unique coalgebra homomorphism $u_\varphi\colon C\rightarrow \underline{\mathrm{coAlg}}(C_1, C_2)$ such that the diagram commutes:
    \[
    \begin{tikzcd}
        C \ar{r}{\widetilde{\varphi}} \ar[dashed]{d}[swap]{\exists !\, u_\varphi} & {[C_1, C_2]}\\
        \underline{\mathrm{coAlg}}(C_1, C_2). \ar{ur}[swap]{\widetilde{\mathrm{ev}}}
    \end{tikzcd}
    \]
    This is making precise the coalgebraic variant of \cref{thm:enriched}: there is a natural identification in $\mathrm{coAlg}$
    \[
    \underline{\mathrm{coAlg}}(C, \underline{\mathrm{coAlg}}(C_1, C_2)) \cong \underline{\mathrm{coAlg}}(C\otimes C_1, C_2)\cong \underline{\mathrm{coAlg}}(C_1, \underline{\mathrm{coAlg}}(C, C_2)).
    \]
    The last identification just signifies there is a symmetry in the coalgebraic case: a $C$-measuring $C\otimes C_1\rightarrow C_2$ can be viewed as a $C_1$-measuring $C_1\otimes C\rightarrow C_2$.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- example-30: body_md -->
\label{ex: partial induction part deux}
    We can strengthen \cref{ex: partial induction} as follows. 
     Given algebras $A$ and $B$ over endofunctor $-+1$, denote by ${\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}_n(A,B)$ the coalgebra $\underline{\mathrm{coAlg}}(\mathbb{n}^\circ, {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,B))$.
     The inclusions $\mathbb{n}^\circ \hookrightarrow (\mathbb{n}+1)^\circ$ define a tower in $\mathrm{coAlg}$:
      \[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=small]
    {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}_\infty(A,B)\ar{r} & \cdots \ar{r} &
    {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}_2(A,B) \ar{r}&
    {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}_1(A,B) \ar{r}&
    {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}_0(A,B).
\end{tikzcd}    
\]
Just as in \cref{ex: partial induction}, we compute that its limit is given by ${\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}_\infty(A,B)\coloneqq\underline{\mathrm{coAlg}}(\mathbb N^c, {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,B))$.
The coalgebras ${\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}_n(A,B)$ should be considered as the universal measuring of $n$-partial homomorphisms, while ${\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}_\infty(A,B)$ is \emph{the universal measuring of $\infty$-partial homomorphisms}: these are functions $f_\infty\colon A\rightarrow B$ for which $f_\infty((n+1)_A)=f_\infty(n_A)+1$, and thus are equivalent to total algebra homomorphisms if $A$ is preinitial.
<!-- end example-30 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
\label{remark: generalized tower}
 The previous example suggests the following generalization.
 Denote by $1$ the terminal object of a locally presentable, symmetric monoidal closed category $\mathscr{C}$.
Let $F$ be an accessible lax symmetric monoidal functor.
