The unique map $!\colon F1\rightarrow 1$ in $\mathscr{C}$ determines an algebra structure on $1$.
In fact, $1$ is also the terminal object in $\mathrm{Alg}$. 
The induced map $F!\colon F^21\rightarrow F1$ defines also an algebra structure on $F1$ such that the map $!\colon F1\rightarrow 1$ is homomorphism of $F$-algebras.
More generally, we obtain algebra homomorphisms $F^{n}!\colon F^{n+1}1\rightarrow F^{n}1$ for all $n\geq 0$. 
We have successfully built a tower in $\mathrm{Alg}$:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
\cdots \ar{r} & F^31\ar{r}{F^2!} \ar{r} & F^2 1 \ar{r}{F!} & F1 \ar{r}{!} & 1,
\end{tikzcd}    
\]
the same one that appeared in Ad\'amek's fixed point theorem (\cref{thm:adamek}), but considered in the category $\mathrm{Alg}$ instead of $\mathscr{C}$.
We now apply the dual coalgebra functor $(-)^\circ\colon\mathrm{Alg}^\mathrm{op}\rightarrow \mathrm{coAlg}$ from \cref{ex: dual}.  
We obtain a filtered diagram in $\mathrm{coAlg}$:
\begin{equation}\label{eq: dual of cofree Adamek}
    \begin{tikzcd}
1^\circ \ar{r}{!^\circ} & (F1)^\circ \ar{r}{F!^\circ} & (F^21)^\circ \ar{r}{F^2!^\circ}& (F^3 1)^\circ \ar{r}  & \cdots.  
    \end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}
Denote by $C_\infty$ the colimit of the above diagram in $\mathrm{coAlg}$ (which is always computed in $\mathscr{C}$).
For all $n\geq 0$, given $F$-algebras $A$ and $B$, we define the \emph{$n$-partial measuring coalgebra from $A$ to $B$} to be the coalgebra determined as:
\[
{\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}_n(A, B)\coloneqq \underline{\mathrm{coAlg}}((F^n 1)^\circ, {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A, B)).    
\]   
The \emph{$\infty$-partial measuring coalgebra from $A$ to $B$} is the coalgebra defined as
\[
    {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}_\infty(A, B)\coloneqq \underline{\mathrm{coAlg}}(C_\infty, {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A, B)).   
\]
If we apply the right adjoint functor $\underline{\mathrm{coAlg}}(-, {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A, B))\colon \mathrm{coAlg}^\mathrm{op}\to \mathrm{coAlg}$ to the filtered diagram of \cref{eq: dual of cofree Adamek}, we obtain the tower in $\mathrm{coAlg}$:
 \[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=small]
    {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}_\infty(A,B)\ar{r} & \cdots \ar{r} &
    {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}_2(A,B) \ar{r}&
    {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}_1(A,B) \ar{r}&
    {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}_0(A,B).
\end{tikzcd}    
\]
As right adjoints preserve limits, we indeed obtain that ${\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}_\infty(A,B)$ is the limit of the tower:
\begin{align*}
    {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}_\infty(A,B) & := \underline{\mathrm{coAlg}}(C_\infty, {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A, B))\\
    & = \underline{\mathrm{coAlg}}(\mathrm{colim}_n\, (F^n1)^\circ, {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A, B)) \\
    & \cong \lim_{n}\underline{\mathrm{coAlg}}((F^n1)^\circ, {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,B))\\
    & =\lim_n {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}_n(A,B).    
\end{align*}
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{thm: most general}
    Let $\mathscr{C}$ be a locally presentably and closed symmetric monoidal category.
    Let $F,G\colon \mathscr{C}\to \mathscr{C}$ be accessible endofunctors.
    Assume that $F$ is lax symmetric monoidal, and that $G$ is an $F$-module, in the sense that there is a transformation
    \[ FX \otimes GY \to G( X \otimes Y) \]
    natural in $X,Y$ and satisfying the diagrams of \cite[Def.~39]{yetter}.
Then the category ${\mathrm{Alg}}_{G}$ is enriched, tensored and cotensored over ${\mathrm{coAlg}}_F$.
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
We obtain a convolution algebra ${\mathrm{coAlg}}_F^\mathrm{op} \times {\mathrm{Alg}}_{G} \to {\mathrm{Alg}}_{G}$ by taking a coalgebra $(C,\chi)$ and an algebra $(A, \alpha)$ to the following composite
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
    G[C,A] \ar{r} & {[FC, GA]} \ar{r}{\chi^*} \ar{r} & {[C, FA]} \ar{r}{\alpha_*} & {[C,A]},
\end{tikzcd}    
\]
    where
    the unmarked arrow is the adjunct of the following composite
    \[
    \begin{tikzcd} 
    FC\otimes G([C,A]) \ar{r} & G(C\otimes [C,A]) \ar{r}{G(\mathrm{ev})} & GA
\end{tikzcd}  
    \]
    where $\mathrm{ev}$ denotes evaluation. The action on morphisms is given by the naturality of constituent arrows of this constructed algebra structure. The functoriality is inherited from the functoriality of $[-, -]$. 

    The diagrams of \cite[Def.~39]{yetter} exactly correspond to the opposite 
    \[[-,-]^\mathrm{op} \colon {\mathrm{coAlg}}_F \times {\mathrm{Alg}}_{G}^\mathrm{op} \to {\mathrm{Alg}}_{G}^\mathrm{op},\]
     this functor being a left action in the sense of \cite{hylandetal}.
    Since $[-,A]^\mathrm{op}$ preserves colimits, so does $[-,A]^\mathrm{op} \colon {\mathrm{coAlg}}_F \to {\mathrm{Alg}}_{G}^\mathrm{op}$. Since ${\mathrm{coAlg}}_F$ is locally presentable, and $\mathrm{Alg}_G^\mathrm{op}$ is essentially small, the functor has a right adjoint.
    Thus, by \cite[Prop.~3.1]{hylandetal}, we see that ${\mathrm{Alg}}_{G}^\mathrm{op}$ is enriched, tensored and cotensored in ${\mathrm{coAlg}}_F$. Thus, ${\mathrm{Alg}}_{G}$ is enriched, tensored and cotensored in ${\mathrm{coAlg}}_F$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{theorem: mixed enriched GF over F}
    Suppose that $\mathscr{C}$ is a locally presentable, closed symmetric monoidal category. Suppose $F$ is an accessible lax symmetric monoidal functor.
Let $G\colon\mathscr{C}\rightarrow \mathscr{C}$ be a $\mathscr{C}$-enriched functor. 
Then ${\mathrm{Alg}}_{GF}$ is enriched and cotensored over ${\mathrm{coAlg}}_F$.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
To apply previous result, we only need to show there exists an $F$-module structure on $GF$, that is, we need a certain natural map 
    \[ FX \otimes GFY \to GF( X \otimes Y). \]
    The $\mathscr{C}$-enrichment of $G$ produces a map $X \otimes GY \rightarrow G(X\otimes Y)$ for any objects $X$ and $Y$ in $\mathscr{C}$. Indeed, this is the adjunct of
    \[
    \begin{tikzcd}
        X \ar{r} & {[Y, X\otimes Y]} \ar{r} & {[GY, G(X\otimes Y)]},
    \end{tikzcd}    
    \]
    where the first map is the coevaluation of the internal hom, and the second map is induced by the $\mathscr{C}$-enrichment. We apply this map to $FX$ and $FY$ to get the following composition
    \[ FX \otimes GFY \rightarrow G(FX\otimes FY) \xrightarrow{G \nabla} GF (X \otimes Y).\]
    One can check that this makes the diagrams of \cite[Def.~39]{yetter} commute.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- example-31: body_md -->
If $F(X)=2\times X^\Sigma$, we could consider $G=\mathrm{id}+1$, and thus ${\mathrm{Alg}}_{GF}$ has a nonempty initial object and is enriched in automata.
<!-- end example-31 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
\Cref{thm:enriched} and \cref{theorem: mixed enriched GF over F} appeared in \cite{north2023coinductive}. This current paper contextualizes and provides more details to the original work. 
\Cref{thm: most general} is new and is an extension of the previous results, and moreover, the tower appearing in \cref{remark: generalized tower} provides a new formalization of partial induction that did not appear in \cite{north2023coinductive}. 
\Cref{subsect: general theory of c-initial} below provides also new results that did not appear in \cite{north2023coinductive}.
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
Recall that if $F$ is an endofunctor in $\mathcal{C}$, we can define the free monad $\widetilde{F}$ in $\mathscr{C}$ on $F$, and  the (Eilenberg--Moore) category of $\widetilde{F}$-algebras in $\mathscr{C}$ is equivalent to the category of $F$-algebras $\mathrm{Alg}_F$ in $\mathscr{C}$. A similar dual statement exists for coalgebras over endofunctors.
    Algebras over monads are enriched in coalgebras over comonads given some compatibility \cite[Thm.~6]{grignou}, and our results fit into this framework.
    Given a field $k$, then $k$-algebras are algebras over the free $k$-algebra monad and $k$-coalgebras are coalgebras over the cofree $k$-coalgebra comonad, and thus the results of \cref{sec: sweedler coalgebras} also fit in this framework.
<!-- end remark-11 -->
<!-- definition-22: body_md -->
\label{def: second initial algebra}
    Suppose that $\mathscr{C}$ is locally presentable and closed and that $F$ is accessible.
Given a coalgebra $C$,
    we say an algebra $A$ is a \emph{$C$-initial algebra} \index{$C$-initial algebra} if there exists a unique map $C\rightarrow {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,X)$, for all algebras $X$. That is, $\mu_C (A,X) \cong *$.
The \emph{terminal} $C$-initial algebra \index{terminal $C$-initial algebra} is the terminal object, if it exists, in the subcategory of ${\mathrm{Alg}}$ spanned by the $C$-initial algebras.
<!-- end definition-22 -->
<!-- remark-12: body_md -->
One may wonder what would happen if for a \emph{set} $S$, we defined an $S$-initial algebra to be an algebra $A$ such that there is a unique \emph{function} $S \to {\mathrm{Alg}}(A,X)$ for all $X \in {\mathrm{Alg}}$. But every algebra is an $\emptyset$-initial algebra, and an $S$-initial algebra is an initial algebra for any $S \neq \emptyset$ (because functions $S \to T$ are unique only when $S = \emptyset$ or $T \cong 1$). Thus, we need to consider ${\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,X)$ and not just ${\mathrm{Alg}}(A,X)$ to obtain interesting $C$-initial algebras.
<!-- end remark-12 -->
<!-- example-32: body_md -->
We have shown in \cref{ex: compute partial alg hom} that ${\mathbb {n}}$ is an ${\mathbb {n}^\circ}$-initial algebra.
 Since ${\mathrm{Alg}}(A,X) \cong {\mathrm{coAlg}}(\mathbb I, {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,X))$, the initial algebra $\mathbb N$ is the $\mathbb I$-initial algebra. In fact, since ${\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(\mathbb N,X) \cong {\mathbb N_\infty}$ for all $X$ by \cref{lem:subobject} or by a similar computation to \cref{ex: compute partial alg hom}, we find that $\mathbb N$ is a $C$-initial algebra for any subterminal coalgebra (i.e., $\emptyset, {\mathbb {n}^\circ}, \mathbb N^c, {\mathbb N_\infty}$).
<!-- end example-32 -->
<!-- example-33: body_md -->
Since the only $\mathbb I$-initial algebra is $\mathbb N$, it is also the terminal $\mathbb I$-initial algebra.
<!-- end example-33 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:map from initial alg to dual}
    Suppose that $\mathscr{C}$ is locally presentable and closed and that $F$ is accessible.
    There is a unique map from any $C$-initial algebra to $C^*$.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
We consider an object $\lim^C\mathrm{id}_{\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}$ with the following universal property:
\[ {\mathrm{Alg}}(A,{\lim}^C\mathrm{id}_{\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}) \cong \lim_{X \in {\mathrm{Alg}}} \ {\mathrm{coAlg}} (C, {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,X)).  \]
(This is the limit of $\mathrm{id}_{\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}$ weighted by the constant functor at $C$.)
Since the hom ${\mathrm{coAlg}} (C, {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,-))$ preserves limits and $\lim_{X \in {\mathrm{Alg}}} X \cong \mathbb N$, we have
\begin{align*}
    \lim_{X \in {\mathrm{Alg}}} \ {\mathrm{coAlg}} (C, {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,X)) &\cong {\mathrm{coAlg}} (C, {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,\lim_{X \in {\mathrm{Alg}}} X)) \\
    &\cong {\mathrm{coAlg}} (C, {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,\mathbb N)) \\
    &\cong {\mathrm{Alg}}(A, [C,\mathbb N]) \\
    &= {\mathrm{Alg}}(A, C^*).
\end{align*}
Thus, $C^*$ has the universal property of $\lim^C\mathrm{id}_{\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}$.

Note that for any $C$-initial algebra $A$, we have $\lim_{X \in {\mathrm{Alg}}} \ {\mathrm{coAlg}} (C, {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,X))$ is the terminal object. Thus, by this universal property of $C^*$, there is a unique map $A \to C^*$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- example-34: body_md -->
Let $C:= {\mathbb {n}^\circ}$. Then elements of $({\mathbb {n}^\circ})^*$ are sequences of $n+1$ natural numbers.
    The successor of a sequence $(a_i)_{i=0}^n$ is $(b_i)_{i=0}^n$ where $b_0 = 0$ and $b_{i+1} = a_i +1$. Notice that the successor of $(b_i)_{i=0}^n$ is $(c_i)_{i=0}^n$ where $c_0 = 0$, $c_1 = 1$ and otherwise $c_{i+2} = a_i +2$. Thus, we can inductively show that the $(n+1)$-st successor of any element of $[{\mathbb {n}^\circ}, \mathbb N]$ is the sequence $(i)_{i=0}^n$, and the successor of this sequence is itself. 

    We claim that the unique morphism $!_{[{\mathbb {n}^\circ}, \mathbb N]} : \mathbb N \to [{\mathbb {n}^\circ}, \mathbb N]$ factors through ${\mathbb {n}}$. We have $m_{[{\mathbb {n}^\circ}, \mathbb N]} = (\min( i,m))_{i=0}^n$. Thus, the restriction of the map $!_{[{\mathbb {n}^\circ}, \mathbb N]}$ to $\{0,...,n\} \subset \mathbb N$ is injective, and $n_{[{\mathbb {n}^\circ}, \mathbb N]} = m_{[{\mathbb {n}^\circ}, \mathbb N]}$ for all $m \geq n$.
<!-- end example-34 -->
<!-- example-35: body_md -->
\label{example: terminal C-initial algebra}
    Now we can show that ${\mathbb {n}}$ is the terminal ${\mathbb {n}^\circ}$-initial algebra. In this calculation, we use the law of excluded middle for the only time in this paper.
    Consider an ${\mathbb {n}^\circ}$-initial algebra $A$.

    First, we show that every $a \in A$ is either the basepoint or a successor. So suppose that there is an element $a \in A$ that is not a basepoint or successor, and consider an algebra $B$ with more than one element. Then for any $b \in B$ and any measure $f: {\mathbb {n}^\circ} \to A \to B$, we can form a measure $\widetilde f: {\mathbb {n}^\circ} \to A \to B$ such that $\widetilde f_n(a) = b$ and $\widetilde f$ agrees with $f$ everywhere else, since \cref{def: partial homomorphism} imposes no requirements on $\widetilde f_n(a)$. Thus, there are multiple measures ${\mathbb {n}^\circ} \to A \to B$, equivalently total algebra homomorphisms ${\mathbb {n}^\circ} \to {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A, B)$, so we find a contradiction.

    Now, we consider the unique map $A \to [{\mathbb {n}^\circ},\mathbb N]$ and claim that this factors through the injection ${\mathbb {n}} \to [{\mathbb {n}^\circ},\mathbb N]$, so that there is a unique $A \to {\mathbb {n}}$. Since every element of $A$ is either a basepoint or a successor, every element of $A$ is either of the form $n_A$ or has infinitely many predecessors. The elements of the form $n_A$ are mapped those to of the form $n_{[{\mathbb {n}^\circ},\mathbb N]}$, and the elements who have infinitely many predecessors can only be mapped to the `top element' $n_{[{\mathbb {n}^\circ},\mathbb N]} = (i)_{i=0}^n$, since this is the only element which has an $m$-th predecessor for any $m \in \mathbb N$. Thus, the unique $A \to [{\mathbb {n}^\circ},\mathbb N]$ indeed factors through ${\mathbb {n}}$.
<!-- end example-35 -->
<!-- example-36: body_md -->
Consider the algebras $(\mathbb N, (\cdot 4)), (\mathbb N, (\cdot 8))$ and the coalgebra $(\mathbb N, (\cdot 2))$.
    A measuring from $(\mathbb N, (\cdot 4))$ to $(\mathbb N, (\cdot 8))$ by $(\mathbb N, (\cdot 2))$ is given by
    \begin{align*}
        \varphi \colon \mathbb N \times \mathbb N &\longrightarrow \mathbb N \\
        (i,j) &\longmapsto i\cdot j^2.
    \end{align*}
    To verify this is a measuring, we must check
    $
    \varphi(i,4j) = 8 \cdot \varphi(2i, j),
    $
    which is the case since
    $$
    \varphi(i,4j) = i \cdot (4j)^2 = 16ij^2 = 8 \cdot 2i \cdot j^2  = 8 \cdot \varphi(2 \cdot i, j).
    $$
<!-- end example-36 -->
<!-- example-37: body_md -->
Consider the algebra $(M, \mathrm{id}_M)$ and the coalgebra $(M,\mathrm{id}_M)$.
    A trivial example of a measuring is the monoid multiplication $\bullet \colon M \times M \to M$.
<!-- end example-37 -->
<!-- example-38: body_md -->
Let $A \in \mathrm{Set}$ be arbitrary and consider the algebra structure on $[A,M]$ given by
    \begin{align*}
        \alpha \colon M &\to [A,M] \\
        m &\mapsto \operatorname{const}_m
    \end{align*}
    and the coalgebra $(M,\mathrm{id}_M)$.
    A measuring from $([A,M], \alpha)$ to itself by $(M,\mathrm{id}_M)$ is given by
    \begin{align*}
        \varphi \colon M \times [A,M] &\longrightarrow [A,M]\\
        (m, f) &\longmapsto (a \mapsto f(a) \bullet m).
    \end{align*}
    Indeed, we can verify
    $
    \varphi(m', \operatorname{const}_m) = \operatorname{const}_{m' \bullet m} = \alpha(m' \bullet m).
    $
<!-- end example-38 -->
<!-- example-39: body_md -->
Let $\gls{List}$ denote the set of finite lists with entries in the monoid $M$.
    We shall be slightly informal in this example, but the 
 the reader can see more precise statements in \cref{subsec:list}.
    We can give it an algebra structure
    $
        \alpha \colon M \to M^*
    $
    by mapping $m$ to the list $[m]$ that contains the single element $m$.
    We can also give it a coalgebra structure
    $
        \chi \colon M^* \to M
    $ 
    by sending a list to the product of all entries in the list.
    If acquainted with functional programming, one might recognize the definition of $\mathtt{fold}$ in the coalgebra structure.

    Let $\gls{EmptList}$ denote the empty list and $\gls{ConcList}$ denote the concatenation of $m \in M$ and $\ell \in M^*$. A measuring from $(M^*,\alpha)$ to itself by $(M^*,\chi)$ is given by
    \begin{align*}
        \varphi \colon M^* \times M^* &\longrightarrow M^*\\
        (\ell', [\:]) &\longmapsto [\:]\\
        (\ell', m:\ell) &\longmapsto (\chi(\ell') \bullet m):\ell,
    \end{align*}
    collapsing the entire list $\ell'$ onto the first element of the list $m:\ell$ using the monoidal structure on $M$.
    To verify this is a measuring we check
    $
    \varphi_{\ell'}(\alpha(m)) = \varphi_{\ell'}([m]) = [\chi(\ell')\bullet m] = \alpha(\chi(\ell')\bullet m).
    $

    Note this is not the only measuring we could have defined.
    Another measuring is given by
    \begin{align*}
        \varphi' \colon M^* \times M^* &\longrightarrow M^*\\
        \ell', [\:] &\longmapsto [\:]\\
        \ell', m:\ell &\longmapsto [\chi(\ell') \bullet m],
    \end{align*}
    simply ignoring the last part of the list $m:\ell$.
    Again we can verify this is a measuring, using the exact same equation as before to find
    $
    \varphi_{\ell'}(\alpha(m)) = \varphi_{\ell'}([m]) = [\chi(\ell')\bullet m] = \alpha(\chi(\ell')\bullet m).
    $
<!-- end example-39 -->
<!-- example-40: body_md -->
Notice that the algebra structures involved can be quite limiting.
We claim there does not exist a total algebra morphism $f\colon\mathbb{n} \to \mathbb N$.
Denoting the algebra structure of $\mathbb{n}$ by $\alpha_n \colon 1 + \mathbb{n} \to \mathbb{n}$, we can create a contradiction by noting that for $n \in \mathbb{n}$, we must have
$
f(n) = f(\alpha_n(n)) = 1 + f(n)
$
which cannot be the case.
However, we are able to define a measuring from $\mathbb{n}$ to $\mathbb N$.
We define the measuring
\begin{align*}
    \varphi \colon {\mathbb{n}}^\circ \times \mathbb{n} &\to \mathbb N \\
    (i,j) &\mapsto \min(i,j).
\end{align*}
We note that checking this is a measuring can be done by comparing the definition of measuring and that of $\varphi$.
Moreover, comparing with the definition also reveals this morphism is unique.
<!-- end example-40 -->
<!-- example-41: body_md -->
Say we would like to define a measuring $\varphi\colon \mathbb{n}^\circ \times (\mathbb{n}-1) \to \mathbb N$.
    By definition $\varphi$ must satisfy
    \begin{align*}
        \varphi(0,j) &= 0 && \text{ for all } j \in \mathbb{n}-1\\
        \varphi(i,0) &= 0 && \text{ for all } i \in \mathbb{n}^\circ\\
        \varphi(i,\alpha_{n-1}(j)) &= 1 + \varphi(i-1, j) && \text{ for all } i \neq 0, j \in \mathbb{n}-1. 
    \end{align*}
    This forces the definition of $\varphi$ to be $\varphi(i,j) = \min(i,j)$ for all $0 \leq i,j \leq n-1$.
    However, we run into contradictions when computing $\varphi(n,n-1)$.
    Since $\alpha_{n-1}(n-2) = \alpha_{n-1}(n-1) = n-1$, we must have that
    $$
    \varphi(n,n-1) = \varphi(n,\alpha_{n-1}(n-2)) = 1 + \varphi(n-1, n-2) = 1 + \min(n-1,n-2) = n-1,
    $$
    but also
    $$
    \varphi(n,n-1) = \varphi(n,\alpha_{n-1}(n-1)) = 1 + \varphi(n-1, n-1) = 1 + \min(n-1,n-1) = n.
    $$
    We see there does not exist a measuring $\varphi \colon \mathbb{n}^\circ \times (\mathbb{n}-1) \to \mathbb N$.
    This is due to the fact that we tried to take the inductive definition of $\varphi$ one step too far.
<!-- end example-41 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
Let $A$ be a $\mathbb{n}^\circ$-initial algebra. Then $A$ is also $(\mathbb{n}-1)^\circ$ initial.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Consider the coalgebra morphism $m \colon (\mathbb{n}-1)^\circ \to \mathbb{n}^\circ, i \mapsto i$.
    This induces a morphism
    \begin{align*}
        m\triangleright A \colon (\mathbb{n}-1)^\circ \triangleright A &\to  \mathbb{n}^\circ \triangleright A \\
        [n,i,a] &\mapsto [n,i,a].
    \end{align*}
    This morphism is monomorphic by definition.
    Since $A$ is $\mathbb{n}^\circ$-initial, we know $\mathbb{n} \triangleright A$ is an initial object.
    This means $m\triangleright A $ is a monomorphism into the initial object, hence an isomorphism.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
Let $A$ be a $\mathbb{n}^\circ$-initial algebra. Then $A$ is also $\mathbb{k}^\circ$ initial for all $k \leq n$.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
Let $A$ be a $\mathbb{n}^\circ$-initial algebra and let $\varphi \colon \mathbb{n}^\circ \times A \to \mathbb N$ be the unique measuring from $A$ to $\mathbb N$ by $\mathbb{n}^\circ$.
    Then for all $i \in \mathbb{n}^\circ$ and $0 \leq j \leq n-i$ we have
    $$
    \varphi(i,a) = \varphi(i, \varphi(i+j, a)_A).
    $$
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Let $k\leq n$.
    Define the coalgebra morphism
    \begin{align*}
        p_j \colon \mathbb{k}^\circ &\to \mathbb{n}^\circ \times \mathbb{n}^\circ \\
        i &\mapsto (i,i+j)
    \end{align*}
    for all $0 \leq j \leq n-k$.
    Consider the composition of measurings $\varphi \circ (\mathrm{id} \times -_{A} \circ \varphi) \in \mu_{\mathbb{n}^\circ \times \mathbb{n}^\circ}(A,\mathbb N)$.
    We can precompose this measuring with the coalgebra morphism $p_j$ to obtain a measuring
    $$
    \mathbb{k}^\circ \times A \xrightarrow{p_j \times \mathrm{id}_A} \mathbb{n}^\circ \times \mathbb{n}^\circ \times A \xrightarrow{\varphi \circ (\mathrm{id} \times -_{A} \circ \varphi)} \mathbb N.
    $$
    We also have the coalgebra morphism $f\colon \mathbb{k}^\circ  \to \mathbb{n}^\circ, i \mapsto i$ which we can precompose with $\varphi$.
    This gives us a measuring
    $$
    \mathbb{k}^\circ \times A \xrightarrow{f \times \mathrm{id}_A} \mathbb{n}^\circ \times A \xrightarrow{\varphi} \mathbb N.
    $$  
    Since $A$ is also $\mathbb{k}^\circ$-initial, we know these measurings must coincide.
    Hence we can state
    $
    \varphi(i,a) = \varphi(i,-_{A} \circ \varphi(i+j,a))
    $
    for all $i \in \mathbb{k}^\circ$ and $0 \leq j \leq n-k$.
    The only restriction placed on $k$ was that $k \leq n$.
    Iterating over all $0 \leq k \leq n$, we arrive at the desired result
    $$
    \varphi(i,a) = \varphi(i,-_{A}\circ \varphi(i+j,a))
    $$
    for all $0 \leq i \leq n$ and $0 \leq j \leq n-i$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:bound}
    Let $A$ be $\mathbb{n}^\circ$-initial and let $\varphi$ be the unique measuring to $\mathbb N$.
    For all $i \in \mathbb{n}^\circ$ and $a \in A$, $\varphi(i,a) \leq i$.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Since $\varphi(i,a) = \varphi(i, (\varphi(i, a))_A)$ by the previous lemma, we know
    $
    [0,i,a] = [0, i, (\varphi(i, a))_A]
    $
    in $\mathbb{n}^\circ \triangleright A$.
    We also have $[\varphi(i,a),z] = [0,i,a]$, and by definition of the equivalence relation $\sim$, we have
    $
    [0, i, (\varphi(i, a))_A] = [\min(i, \varphi(i, a)), z].
    $
    From this we conclude
    $$
    \varphi(i,a) = \min(i, \varphi(i, a)),
    $$
    hence $\varphi(i,a) \leq i$ for all $i \in \mathbb{n}^\circ$.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:Atonexists}
Let $A$ be an  $\mathbb{n}^\circ$-initial algebra.
Let $\varphi\colon \mathbb{n}^\circ\times A\rightarrow \mathbb N$ be the unique measuring. The functions $\varphi_k \colon A \to \mathbb{k}$ 
are total algebra morphisms for all $0 \leq k \leq n$.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
We proceed by induction over $k$.
    For $k = 0$, we have that $\mathbb{k} \cong 1$, the terminal object in the category of algebras.
    Hence $\varphi_0 : A \to 1$ is an algebra morphism.
    For the inductive step, assume $\varphi_{k-1} : A \to \mathbb{k}-1$ is an algebra morphism.
    We wish to show $\alpha_k(\varphi_k(a)) = \varphi_k(\alpha(a))$ for all $a \in A$.
    If $\varphi_k(a) = 0$, we know
    \begin{align*}
         \varphi(k,\alpha(a)) & = 1 + \varphi(k-1,a) \\
         &= 1 + \varphi(k-1, (\varphi(k,a))_A) \\
         & = 1 + \varphi(k-1, 0_A) \\
         &  = 1 = \alpha_k(0) \\
         &= \alpha_k(\varphi(k,a)).
    \end{align*}
    If $\varphi_k(a) \geq 0$ we can make the following deduction
    \begin{align*}
        \alpha_k(\varphi_k(a)) 
        &= \alpha_k(\varphi(k, a))\\
        &= 1 + \alpha_{k-1}(\varphi(k,a) - 1)\\
        &= 1 + \alpha_{k-1}(\varphi(k,(\varphi(k,a)) - 1)_A)\\
        &= 1 + \alpha_{k-1}(\varphi(k-1,(\varphi(k,a) - 1)_A))\\
        &= 1 + \varphi(k-1,  \varphi(k,a)_A)\\
        &= 1 + \varphi(k-1, a)\\
        &= \varphi(k,\alpha(a)).
    \end{align*}
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:Atonunique}
    For any $\mathbb{n}^\circ$-initial algebra $A$, there exist at most one algebra morphism $A \to \mathbb{n}$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
By \cref{prop:map from initial alg to dual}, there exists a unique morphism $A \to [\mathbb{n}^\circ, \mathbb N]$ for any $\mathbb{n}^\circ$-initial algebra $A$.
    Since $\mathbb{n}$ is $\mathbb{n}^\circ$-initial we know there exists a unique morphism $m \colon \mathbb{n} \rightarrowtail [\mathbb{n}^\circ, \mathbb N]$.
    Upon closer inspection $m$ turns out to be a monomorphism.
    Given any two morphisms $f,g \colon A \to \mathbb{n}$, we can draw the following diagram
    \[\begin{tikzcd}
        A & {[\mathbb{n}^\circ, \mathbb N]} \\
        & \mathbb{n}
        \arrow["{!}", from=1-1, to=1-2]
        \arrow["f"', shift right, from=1-1, to=2-2]
        \arrow["g", shift left, from=1-1, to=2-2]
        \arrow["m"', tail, from=2-2, to=1-2].
    \end{tikzcd}\]
    Since the morphism $A \to [\mathbb{n}^\circ, \mathbb N]$ is unique, we know the composites $m \circ f = m \circ g$, and by $m$ being mono we conclude $f = g$.
    Hence, there can be at most one algebra morphism from a $\mathbb{n}^\circ$-initial algebra $A$ to $\mathbb{n}$.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
The algebra $\mathbb{n}$ is the terminal $\mathbb{n}^\circ$-initial algebra.
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Given an $\mathbb{n}^\circ$ initial algebra $A$, by Proposition \ref{prop:Atonexists} we obtain an algebra morphism $\varphi_n \colon A \to \mathbb{n}$.
    By Lemma \ref{lem:Atonunique} it is unique.
    We conclude $\mathbb{n}$ is the terminal $\mathbb{n}^\circ$-initial algebra.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- example-42: body_md -->
The first function is the length function $\mathtt{len}$, which takes a list and returns its length.
We want to word it in the language of algebras, so we first define an algebra
\begin{align*}
    1+M \times \mathbb N &\to \mathbb N\\
    * &\mapsto 0\\
    (m, n) &\mapsto n+1.
\end{align*}
The function $\gls{len}$ on lists $\ell \in M^*$ is then given by the unique algebra morphism $M^* \to \mathbb N$.
<!-- end example-42 -->
<!-- example-43: body_md -->
The second function considered takes two lists and concatenates them.
Classically, this would be denoted as a function $M^* \times M^* \to M^*$, but to frame it as an algebra morphism, we consider it as a function $M^* \to [M^*,M^*]$.
To this end, consider the the algebra
\begin{align*}
    \alpha \colon 1+M \times [M^*, M^*] &\to [M^*, M^*]\\
    * &\mapsto \mathrm{id}\\
    (m,f) &\mapsto (\ell \mapsto m:f(\ell)).
\end{align*}
The concatenation function is denoted by $(++)$ and is defined uniquely by the following diagram
\[\begin{tikzcd}
1+M\times M^* & [2em]1+M \times [M^*, M^*] \\
M^* & [M^*, M^*]
            \arrow["F(\:++\:)", from=1-1, to=1-2] 
\arrow["",from=1-1, to=2-1] \arrow["\alpha",from=1-2, to=2-2]
            \arrow["(++)", from=2-1, to=2-2] 
            [M^*, M^*]
\end{tikzcd}\]
where uniqueness follows from the fact $M^*$ is the initial algebra.
Given $\ell \in M^*$, the function $(++)(\ell) \in [M^*,M^*]$ is the function which takes a list $\ell'$ and concatenates it with $\ell$,
resulting in the list $(++)(\ell)(\ell') = \ell ++\: \ell'$.
<!-- end example-43 -->
<!-- example-44: body_md -->
The next function is $\mathtt{head}$, which is a partially defined function which attempts to extract the first element of a list-like.
We define the algebra
\begin{align*}
    \alpha \colon 1 + M \times (M + \{\bot\})&\to M + \{\bot\}\\
    * &\mapsto \bot\\
    (m,\ell) &\mapsto m.
\end{align*}
The function $\mathtt{head}$ is then defined as the following algebra morphism
\begin{align*}
  \mathtt{head} \colon M^* & \to (M + \{\bot\}, \alpha) \\
    [\:] &\mapsto \bot \\
    m:\ell  & \mapsto m.  
\end{align*}
<!-- end example-44 -->
<!-- example-45: body_md -->
The next function is $\mathtt{take}(n)$, which is a function that takes the first $n \in {\mathbb N_\infty}$ elements of a list.
We have already defined this function ``by hand'' when defining the algebra structure on $M^{\leq n}$, but we would like view it from our algebraic perspective.
As maybe suspected, it is given by the unique function
\begin{align*}
    \mathtt{take}(n) \colon M^* &\to  M^{\leq n}\\
    \ell &\mapsto \mathtt{take}(n)(\ell).
\end{align*}
<!-- end example-45 -->
<!-- example-46: body_md -->
The $\mathtt{filter}$ function takes a predicate $p \in P_M \coloneqq [M, \{\top, \bot\}]$ and a list $\ell \in M^*$ and returns only the elements in $\ell$ which satisfy $p$.
Classically, this would be written as $\mathtt{filter}\colon M^* \times P_M \to M^*$, but in our case we want to consider it as a function
$\mathtt{filter}\colon M^* \to [P_M, M^*]$.
First, we define an algebra structure on $ [P_M, M^*]$ by
\begin{align*}
    \beta \colon 1+M\times  [P_M, M^*] &\to  [P_M, M^*] \\
    * &\mapsto \operatorname{const}_{[\:]}\\
    (m,f) &\mapsto \left(
        p \mapsto
        \begin{cases}
            m:f(p) \text{ if } p(m)\\
            f(p) \text{ otherwise}
        \end{cases}
        \right).
\end{align*}
The function $\mathtt{filter}$ is given by the unique algebra morphism $M^* \to  [P_M, M^*]$.
Another way to construct the filter function using a predicate $p \in P_M$ is to compute the set $M_p = \{m \in M \mid p(m) = \top\}$.
Since $M_p \subset M$, $M_p^*$ has the algebra structure corresponding to filtering.
The function $\mathtt{filter}(p)$ is given by the unique function $\mathtt{filter}(p) \colon M^* \to M_p^*$.
<!-- end example-46 -->
<!-- example-47: body_md -->
\label{ex:meauringtoX^*}
Give any commutative monoid $(M,e,\bullet)$, we remark there does not exist a total algebra morphism $f\colon M^{\leq n} \to M^*$, since for a list $\ell \in M^{\leq n}$ of length $n$, we must have that
$$
m : f(\mathtt{take}(n-1)(\ell)) = f(m:\mathtt{take}(n-1)(\ell)) = f(m:\ell) = m:f(\ell),
$$
which cannot be the case.
Note that in the above computation we have used $\mathtt{take}(n)(m:\ell) = m:\mathtt{take}(n-1)(\ell)$.
The problem here is that we are disregarding the last element of the list, where an algebra morphism into $M^*$ does need that information.

However, we are able to define a measuring from $M^{\leq n}$ to $M^*$.
We define the measuring
\begin{align*}
    \varphi \colon ({M^{\leq n}})^\circ \times M^{\leq n} &\to M^* \\
    ([\:], \ell) &\mapsto [\:]\\
    (\ell', [\:]) &\mapsto [\:]\\
    (m':\ell',m:\ell) &\mapsto (m' \bullet m) : \varphi(\ell', \ell).
\end{align*}
We note that checking this is a measuring can be done by comparing the definition of measuring and that of $\varphi$.
This example is valid because the coalgebra ${(M^{\leq n})}^\circ$ limits up to which point we are considering elements of the algebra $M^{\leq n}$.
The problem we had earlier, caused by disregarding the last element of a list due to the maximum length of the list, is mitigated by the introduction of the coalgebra ${(M^{\leq n})}^\circ$.
Since the elements of ${(M^{\leq n})}^\circ$ all have length at most $n$, we can truly disregard the last element of a list whenever its length exceeds $n$.
<!-- end example-47 -->
<!-- example-48: body_md -->
Next, we investigate another interesting preinitial algebra given by $(M')^*$ for some subset $M' \subseteq M$.
We would like to find a measuring $\varphi\colon C \times (M')^* \to B$ for some coalgebra $C \in \mathrm{coAlg}$ and some algebra $B \in \mathrm{Alg}$.
This measuring must satisfy
$$
\varphi_c(m:\ell) = 
\begin{cases}
    \beta((m\bullet m'), \varphi_{c'}(\ell)) \text{ if } \chi(c) = (m',c') \\
    e_B \text{ otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$
By the coalgebra structure on $(M')^*$, we have that for any $m \not\in M'$, $m:\ell = \ell$.
In the case that $\chi(c) = (m',c')$ and $m \not\in M'$, the above condition becomes
$
\varphi_c(\ell) = \varphi_c(m:\ell) = \beta((m\bullet m'), \varphi_{c'}(\ell)),
$
giving us a contradiction since we need $\varphi_c(\ell) = \beta((m\bullet m'), \varphi_{c'}(\ell))$ for all $m \not\in M'$.
The problem here is a loss of information. 
This loss stems from the fact that $m:m:\dots:m:\ell = \ell$ whenever $m \not\in M'$,
whereas the measuring does need to take into account the added elements $m$.
<!-- end example-48 -->
<!-- example-49: body_md -->
Using measurings, we are also able to define a more flexible version of the $\mathtt{map}$ function.
    Traditionally, $\mathtt{map}$ takes a function $f$ and a list and applies $f$ to all elements of the list element wise.
    Using measurings, we can actually specify a list of functions which gets applied to elements of a list in a pairwise fashion.
    For each $m \in M$, define the function $r_m \colon M \to M$ which multiplies an element of $M$ by $m$ from the right.
    We define the algebra
    \begin{align*}
        1+ M \times [M,M]^{\leq \infty} &\longrightarrow [M,M]^{\leq \infty}\\
        * &\longmapsto r_e\\
        (m,\ell) &\longmapsto r_m : \ell.
    \end{align*}
    We can now define the measuring
    \begin{align*}
        \varphi \colon {M^*}^\circ \times  [M,M]^{\leq \infty} &\to M^* \\
        ([\:], \ell) &\mapsto [\:]\\
        (\ell, [\:]) &\mapsto [\:]\\
        (m:\ell, f:k) &\mapsto f(m):\varphi(\ell, k).
    \end{align*}
    We verify this is a measuring by checking
    $
    \varphi(m':\ell, r_{m}:k) = r_{m}(m'):\varphi(\ell, k) = (m'\bullet m) :\varphi(\ell,k).
    $
    Note that we really need to define an algebra structure on $[M,M]^{\leq \infty}$ instead of a coalgebra structure, since there is no obvious way to extract $m \in M$ from a function $f \colon M \to M$ in such a way that the conditions on a measuring are satisfied.
<!-- end example-49 -->
<!-- example-50: body_md -->
We would like to calculate $\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}(M^{\leq n}, B)$ for arbitrary $B \in \mathrm{Alg}$.
Our aim is to leverage the isomorphism
$$
\mathrm{coAlg}(C, \underline{\mathrm{Alg}}(M^{\leq n}, B)) \cong \mu_C(M^{\leq n}, B) \cong \mathrm{Alg}(M^{\leq n}, [C,B]).
$$
To do so, we make an observation about $\mathrm{Alg}(M^{\leq n}, Z)$ for an arbitrary algebra $(Z, \zeta) \in \mathrm{Alg}$.
Since $M^{\leq n}$ is preinitial, any morphism out of $M^{\leq n}$ is unique.
So, $\mathrm{Alg}(M^{\leq n}, Z)$ has at most one element.
The question now becomes if there is a condition on $Z$ for $\mathrm{Alg}(M^{\leq n}, Z)$ to be inhabited.
We claim this condition is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:condition}
    \zeta(m, 
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{Z}(\ell)) = \zeta(m, 
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{Z}(\mathtt{take}(n-1)(\ell))) \text { for all } (m,\ell) \in M\times M^{\leq n}.
\end{equation}
Notice that $\mathtt{take}(n-1)(\ell) = \ell$ for all lists of length less than $n$, so the only non-trivial case is when $\mathtt{len}(\ell) = n$.
If \cref{eq:condition} is satisfied, we claim the unique algebra morphism $M^{\leq n} \to Z$ is given by
$$
 
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{Z} \circ \iota\colon M^{\leq n} \hookrightarrow M^* \to Z,
$$
where $\iota \in [M^{\leq n}, M^*]$ is an inclusion of sets, not an algebra morphism.
For brevity, we will write $ 
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{Z} \circ \iota =  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{Z}$ if the domain is understood.
To verify this is an algebra morphism, we must check it commutes with the algebra structures.
If we denote the algebra structure on $M^{\leq n}$ by $\alpha_n$, we need to check
$
 
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{Z}(\alpha_n(m,\ell)) = \zeta(m,  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{Z}(\ell)),
$
since the case of the empty list is trivial.
Using \cref{eq:condition} and that $ 
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{Z}\colon M^* \to Z$ is an algebra morphism we can make the following deduction:
\begin{align*}
    ( 
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{Z}\circ \iota)(\alpha_n(m,\ell)) 
    &= ( 
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{Z} \circ \iota)(m:\mathtt{take}(n-1)(\ell)) \\
    &=  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{Z}(m:\mathtt{take}(n-1)(\ell)) \\
    &= \zeta(m,  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{Z}(\mathtt{take}(n-1)(\ell))) \\
    &= \zeta(m, 
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{Z}(\ell))\\
    &= \zeta(m,( 
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{Z} \circ \iota)(\ell)).
\end{align*}
Conversely, if there exists $\ell \in M^{\leq n}$ such that $\zeta(m, 
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{Z}(\ell)) \neq \zeta(m, 
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{Z}(\mathtt{take}(n-1)(\ell)))$ it is impossible to construct an algebra morphism $f\colon M^{\leq n} \to Z$.
This can be seen by trying to construct such a morphism $f$ and observing $f(\alpha_n(m,\ell)) \neq \zeta(m,f(\ell))$ in this case.

Now that we have an indication on whether $\mathrm{Alg}(M^{\leq n}, Z)$ is inhabited for arbitrary $Z \in \mathrm{Alg}$, we can focus in $Z = [C,B]$.
Observing the algebra structure on $[C,B]$, we see the morphism $ 
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{[C,B]}$ is given by
\begin{align*}
     
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{[C,B]} \colon M^* &\to [C,B] \\
    [\:] &\mapsto (c \mapsto e_B)\\
    m:\ell &\mapsto 
    \left(
        c \mapsto
        \begin{cases}
            \beta(m \bullet m',  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{[C,B]}(\ell)(c')) \text{ if } \chi(c) = (m',c') \\
            e_B \text{ if } \chi(c) = *.
        \end{cases}
    \right).
\end{align*}
Denoting the algebra structure on $[C,B]$ by $\alpha$, we would like to know under which condition on $C$ and $B$ $\alpha(m,  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{[C,B]}(\ell)) = \alpha(m, 
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{[C,B]}(\mathtt{take}(n-1)(\ell)))$.
Unpacking the above, we find this is the case if
$$
\beta(m\bullet m',  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{[C,B]}(\ell)(c')) = \beta(m\bullet m',  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{[C,B]}(\mathtt{take}(n-1)(\ell))(c')) 
$$
for all $(m',c') \in \operatorname{im}(\chi)$.
By definition of $ 
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{[C,B]}$, the above condition can be satisfied if $\mathtt{len}(c) \leq n$ for all $c\in C$ or if condition \cref{eq:condition} holds for $B$.
So, we have the following:
$$
\mathrm{Alg}(M^{\leq n}, [C,B]) \cong 
\begin{cases}
    \{*\} \text{ if } \beta(m, 
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{B}(\ell)) = \beta(m, 
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{B}(\mathtt{take}(n-1)(\ell)))\,
    \\ \hspace{9em} \forall (m,\ell) \in M \times M^{\leq n}\\
    \{*\} \text{ if } \mathtt{len}(c) \leq n \text{ for all } c \in C\\
    \emptyset \text{ otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$
Now we can make use the fact that $\mathrm{coAlg}(C, \underline{\mathrm{Alg}}(M^{\leq n}, B)) \cong \mathrm{Alg}(M^{\leq n}, [C,B])$.
We observe that in the case of $\beta(m, 
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{B}(\ell)) = \beta(m, 
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{B}(\mathtt{take}(n-1)(\ell)))$, the object $\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}(M^{\leq n}, B)$ has the universal property of the terminal coalgebra $M^{\leq \infty}$.
Whenever this is not the case, $\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}(M^{\leq n}, B)$ has the universal property of $M^{\leq n} \in \mathrm{coAlg}$.
                                                                        
We conclude
$$
\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}(M^{\leq n}, B) = 
\begin{cases}
    M^{\leq \infty} \text{ if }  \beta(m, 
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{B}(\ell)) = \beta(m, 
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{B}(\mathtt{take}(n-1)(\ell))), \\ \hspace{10em} \forall (m,\ell) \in M \times M^{\leq n}\\
    M^{\leq n} \text{ otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$
<!-- end example-50 -->
<!-- example-51: body_md -->
For similar reasons as in \cref{ex:meauringtoX^*}, we remark there does not exist an algebra morphism $T_{M,n} \to T_M$.
    There does however exist a measuring from $T_{M,n}$ to $T_M$ by $T_{M,n}^\circ$.
    It is given by
    \begin{align*}
        \varphi\colon T_{M,n}^\circ \times T_{M,n} &\to T_{M} \\
        (e_T, (m,\ell, r)) &\mapsto e_T\\
        ((m',\ell', r'), e_T) &\mapsto e_T\\
        ((m',\ell',r') , (m,\ell, r)) &\mapsto y (m' \bullet m,\varphi(\ell', \ell), \varphi(r',r)),
    \end{align*}
    which is a measuring by definition.
    Again, for reasons similar to those seen in \cref{ex:meauringtoX^*} a measuring to $T_M$ does exist, where an algebra morphism does not.
    The coalgebra $T_{M,n}^\circ$ gives us control over which parts of an element in $T_{M,n}$ we consider.
<!-- end example-51 -->
<!-- example-52: body_md -->
If we only care about modifying the shape of an element in $T_M$ and don't want to introduce any twist, we can consider the measuring
    \begin{align*}
        \varphi \colon T_{\{e\}}^\circ \times T_M &\to T_M \\
        (e_T, (m,\ell, r)) &\mapsto e_T\\
        ((e,\ell', r'), e_T) &\mapsto e_T\\
        ((e,\ell',r') , (m,\ell, r)) &\mapsto y (m,\varphi(\ell', \ell), \varphi(r',r)),
    \end{align*}
    which is a measuring by definition.
    This measuring takes a tree containing only the unit of the monoid $t' \in T_{\{e\}}^\circ$ and uses its shape to modify a tree $t \in T_M$ to fit within the shape of $t'$.
<!-- end example-52 -->
<!-- example-53: body_md -->
Again, we can generalize the map function using a measuring to obtain more fine grained control over which function gets applied to which elements.
    Recall we define the function $r_m\colon M \to M$ as multiplication by $m$ on the right.
    Let $[M,M]$ be the set of functions $M \to M$, and let $T_{[M,M]}$ be the set of all binary trees with labels in $[M,M]$.
    We can then define an algebra structure on $T_{[M,M]}$ by
    \begin{align*}
        1 + M \times T_{[M,M]} \times T_{[M,M]} &\to T_{[M,M]} \\
        * &\mapsto e_T\\
        (m,\ell,r) &\mapsto (r_m, \ell, r).
    \end{align*}
    Now we have a measuring given by
    \begin{align*}
        \varphi\colon T_M^\circ \times T_{[M,M]} &\to T_M \\
        (e_T, (f, \ell, r)) &\mapsto e_T\\
        ((m', \ell', r'), e_T) &\mapsto e_T\\
        ((m', \ell', r'), (f, \ell, r)) &\mapsto (f(m), \varphi(\ell',\ell), \varphi(r',r)).
    \end{align*}
    To check this is a measuring, we verify
    $$
    \varphi((m', \ell', r'), (r_m, \ell, r)) =  (r_m(m'), \varphi(\ell',\ell), \varphi(r',r)) =  (m' \bullet m, \varphi(\ell',\ell), \varphi(r',r)).
    $$
<!-- end example-53 -->
<!-- example-54: body_md -->
For similar reasons as in previous examples, we remark there does not exist an algebra morphism $S_{M,n} \to S_M$.
    There does however exist a measuring from $S_{M,n}$ to $S_M$ by $S_{M,n}^\circ$.
    It is given by
    \begin{align*}
        \varphi\colon S_{M,n}^\circ \times S_{M,n} &\to S_{M} \\
        (e_S, (m,\ell)) &\mapsto e_S\\
        ((m',\ell'), e_T) &\mapsto e_T\\
        ((m',\ell') , (m,\ell)) &\mapsto (m' \bullet m,\,\mathtt{map}(\varphi)(\mathtt{zip}(\ell',\ell))),
    \end{align*}
    which is a measuring by definition.
    Again, reasoning similar to that seen in Example \ref{ex:meauringtoX^*} applies as to why a measuring to $S_M$ does exist, where an algebra morphism does not.
    The coalgebra $S_{M,n}^\circ$ gives us control over which parts of an element in $S_{M,n}$ we consider.
<!-- end example-54 -->
<!-- example-55: body_md -->
Consider the measuring
    \begin{align*}
        \varphi\colon S_{\{e\}}^\circ \times S_M &\to S_M \\
        (e_S, (m,\ell)) &\mapsto e_S\\
        ((e,\ell'), e_T) &\mapsto e_T\\
        ((e,\ell') , (m,\ell)) &\mapsto (m,\mathtt{map}(\varphi)(\mathtt{zip}(\ell',\ell))),
    \end{align*}
    which is a measuring by definition.
    This measuring takes a tree containing only the unit of the monoid $t' \in S_1^\circ$ and uses its shape to modify a tree $t \in S_M$ to fit within the shape of $t'$.
<!-- end example-55 -->
<!-- example-56: body_md -->
Again, we can generalize the map function using a measuring to obtain more fine grained control over which function gets applied to which elements.
    Recall we define the function $r_m\colon M \to M$ as multiplication by $m$ on the right.
    We define an algebra structure on $S_{[M,M]}$ by
    \begin{align*}
        1 + M \times S_{[M,M]} \times S_{[M,M]} &\to S_{[M,M]} \\
        * &\mapsto e_T\\
        (m,\ell,r) &\mapsto (r_m, \ell, r).
    \end{align*}
    Now we have a measuring given by
    \begin{align*}
        \varphi\colon S_M^\circ \times S_{[M,M]} &\to S_M \\
        (e_S, (f, \ell)) &\mapsto e_S\\
        ((m', \ell'), e_S) &\mapsto e_S\\
        ((m', \ell'), (f, \ell)) &\mapsto (f(m'), \mathtt{map}(\varphi)(\mathtt{zip}(\ell',\ell))).
    \end{align*}
    To check this is a measuring, we verify
    $$
    \varphi((m', \ell'), (r_m, \ell)) =  (r_m(m'), \mathtt{map}(\varphi)(\mathtt{zip}(\ell',\ell))) =  (m' \bullet m, \mathtt{map}(\varphi)(\mathtt{zip}(\ell',\ell))).
    $$
<!-- end example-56 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
Let $A$ be a $S_{M,n}^\circ$-initial algebra. Then $A$ is also $S_{M,n-1}^\circ$ initial.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Consider the coalgebra morphism $\iota\colon S_{M,n-1}^\circ \to S_{M,n}^\circ, s \mapsto s$.
    This induces a morphism
    \begin{align*}
        \iota\triangleright A \colon S_{M,n-1}^\circ \triangleright A &\to  S_{M,n}^\circ \triangleright A \\
        [e_{\operatorname{Fr}}] &\mapsto [e_{\operatorname{Fr}}]\\
        [s,a] &\mapsto [s,a]\\
        [m,\ell] &\mapsto [m, \mathtt{map}(\iota \triangleright A)(\ell)].
    \end{align*}
    This morphism is monomorphic by definition.
    Since $A$ is $S_{M,n}^\circ$-initial, we know $S_{M,n} \triangleright A$ is an initial object.
    This means $\iota\triangleright A $ is a monomorphism into the initial object, hence an isomorphism.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
Let $A$ be a $S_{M,n}^\circ$-initial algebra. Then $A$ is also $S_{M,k}^\circ$ initial for all $k \leq n$.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:adddepth}
    Let $A$ be a $S_{M,n}^\circ$-initial algebra and let $\varphi\colon S_{M,n}^\circ \times A \to S_M$ be the unique measuring from $A$ to $S_{M}$ by $S_{M,n}^\circ$.
    For all $0 \leq i \leq n$, let  $s_i \in S_{M,n}$ be the largest tree of depth $i$ in $S_{M,n}$ which contains only the unit $e \in M$.
    Then for all $0 \leq i \in n$ and $0 \leq j \leq n-i$ we have
    $$
    \varphi_{s_i}(a) = \varphi_{s_i}( 
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A}\circ\varphi_{s_{i+j}} (a)).
    $$
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Let $k\leq n$.
    First, we define a function which takes two trees and appends the second tree to all the roots of the first tree.
    We define it as
    \begin{align*}
        (++) \colon S_{M,\infty} \times S_{M,\infty} &\to S_{M,\infty} \\
        (e_S, s) &\mapsto s\\
        ((m, \ell), s) &\mapsto (m, \mathtt{map}( (++) s )(\ell)).
    \end{align*}
    For all $0 \leq j \leq n-k$, define the coalgebra morphism
    \begin{align*}
        p_j\colon S_{M,k}^\circ &\to S_{M,n}^\circ \times S_{M,n}^\circ \\
        s &\mapsto (s,\widetilde{s} ++ s_j),
    \end{align*}
    where $\widetilde{s}$ is the unique tree $\widetilde{s} \in S_{\{e\}, k}$ such that $\mathtt{shape}(\widetilde{s}) = \mathtt{shape}(s)$.
                                              
    Consider the composition of measurings $\varphi \circ (\mathrm{id} \times  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A} \circ \varphi) \in \mu_{S_{M,n}^\circ \times S_{M,n}^\circ}(A,S_{M})$.
    We can precompose this measuring with the coalgebra morphism $p_j$ to obtain a measuring
    $$
    S_{M,k}^\circ \times A \xrightarrow{p_j \times \mathrm{id}_A} S_{M,n}^\circ \times S_{M,n}^\circ \times A \xrightarrow{\varphi \circ (\mathrm{id} \times  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A} \circ \varphi)} S_{M}.
    $$
               
    We also have the coalgebra morphism $\iota\colon S_{M,k}^\circ  \to S_{M,n}^\circ, s \mapsto s$ which we can precompose with $\varphi$.
    This gives us a measuring
    $$
    S_{M,k}^\circ \times A \xrightarrow{\iota \times \mathrm{id}_A} S_{M,n}^\circ \times A \xrightarrow{\varphi} S_{M}.
    $$  
    Since $A$ is also $S_{M,k}^\circ$-initial, we know these measurings must coincide.
    Hence we can state
    $
    \varphi(s,a) = \varphi(s, 
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A} \circ \varphi(\widetilde{s} ++ s_j,a))
    $
    for all $s \in S_{M,k}^\circ$ and $0 \leq j \leq n-k$.
    The only restriction placed on $k$ was that $k \leq n$.
    Iterating over all $0 \leq k \leq n$, we arrive at the desired result
    $$
    \varphi(s,a) = \varphi(s, 
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A}\circ \varphi(\widetilde{s} ++ s_j,a))
    $$
    for all $0 \leq i \leq n$ and $0 \leq j \leq n-i$.
    In particular this holds for $s = s_i$, and noting $s_i ++ s_j = s_{i + j}$ we obtain the desired result.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:bound}
    Let $A$ be $S_{M,n}^\circ$-initial and let $\varphi$ be the unique measuring to $S_{M}$.
    For all $0 \leq i \leq n$ and $a \in A$, we have $\varphi(s_i,a) \in S_{M,i}$.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
We will proceed by induction over $i$.
    For the base case $i = 0$, we have $s_0 = e_S$, so $\varphi(s_0, a) = e_S \in S_{M,0}$.
    For the induction step, assume $\varphi(s_i, a) \in S_{M,i}$.
    Using $s_{i+1} = (e,(s_i)^{(\infty)})$ and the previous lemma we can write
    $
    \varphi(s_{i+1}, a) = \varphi( (e,(s_i)^{(\infty)}),  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A}(\varphi(s_{i+1}, a))).
    $
    Let $\alpha\colon 1 + M \times (S_M)^{\leq \infty} \to S_M$, then we can write $(m,s) = \alpha^{-1}(\varphi(s_{i+1}, a))$ where $s$ is the list with components $s_i$.
    We then know by definition of a measuring that
    $$
    \varphi(s_{i+1}, a)  = \varphi( (e,(s_i)^{(\infty)}),  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A}(\varphi(s_{i+1}, a))) = 
    (e \bullet m, \mathtt{map}(\varphi)(\mathtt{zip}((s_i)^{(\infty)}, k)   ) ),
    $$
    where $k = \mathtt{map}( 
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A})(s)$.
    By the induction hypothesis, we know $$\mathtt{map}(\varphi)(\mathtt{zip}((s_i)^{(\infty)}, k)   )  \in (S_{M,i})^{\leq \infty},$$ hence $\varphi(s_{i+1}, a) \in S_{M,i + 1}$ by definition.
    This concludes the induction step and the proof.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- definition-23: body_md -->
\label{def:AtoS_k}
    Let $A$ be $S_{M,n}^\circ$-initial, let $\varphi$ be the unique measuring to $S_{M}$ and let $0 \leq k \leq n$. Define the functions
    \begin{align*}
        \varphi_k \colon A &\to S_{M,k} \\
        a &\mapsto \varphi(s_k,a),
    \end{align*}
    which are well-defined by the previous corollary.
<!-- end definition-23 -->
<!-- remark-13: body_md -->
With this new definition, we can restate  \cref{lem:adddepth} as
    $$
    \varphi_i = \varphi_i \circ  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A} \circ \varphi_{i+j}
    $$
    for all $0 \leq i \leq n$ and $0 \leq j \leq n-i$.
<!-- end remark-13 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:AtoS_nexists}
    The functions $\varphi_k\colon A \to S_{M,k}$ from  \cref{def:AtoS_k} are algebra morphisms for all $0 \leq k \leq n$.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
We proceed by induction over $k$.
    For $k = 0$, we have that $S_{M,k} \cong 1$, the terminal object in $\mathrm{Set}$.
    Hence $\varphi_0\colon A \to S_{M,0}$ is an algebra morphism.
    For the inductive step, assume $\varphi_{k-1}\colon A \to S_{M,k-1}$ is an algebra morphism.
    We wish to show $\varphi_k$ is an algebra morphism.
    In more detail, we aim to show $$\alpha_k(m, \mathtt{map}(\varphi_k)(\ell)) = \varphi_k(\alpha(m,\ell))$$ for all $(m,\ell) \in M \times A^{\leq \infty}$.
    First, we will write $\ell = (a_i)_{i = 0}^j$, where $j \in {\mathbb N_\infty}$.
    We can now write
    \begin{align*}
        \alpha_k(m, \mathtt{map}(\varphi_k)(\ell))
        &= \alpha_k(m, \mathtt{map}(\varphi_k)((a_i)_i))\\
        &= \alpha_k(m, (\varphi_k(a_i))_i)\\
        &= \alpha_k(m, (\varphi_k \circ  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A} \circ \varphi_k(a_i))_i).
    \end{align*}
    Writing $\varphi_k \circ  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A} \circ \varphi_k(a_i) = t_i$, we can make the case distinction
    $$ 
    t_i = 
    \begin{cases}
        e_S &\text{ if } \varphi_k(a_i) = e_S \in S_M \\
        (m_i, \mathtt{map}(\varphi_{k-1} \circ  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A})(a_i)) &\text{ if } \varphi_k(a_i) = (m_i,a_i) \in S_M
    \end{cases}
    $$
    by $\varphi \colon S_{M,n}^\circ \times A \to S_M$ being a measuring.
    This means $$\alpha_k(m, \mathtt{map}(\varphi_k)(\ell)) = \alpha_k(m, (t_i)_i).$$
    By the algebra structure of $S_{M,k}$, we can write this as
    $
    \alpha_k(m, (t_i)_i) = (m,(r_i)_i),
    $
    where
    $$
    r_i = 
    \begin{cases}
        e_S &\text{ if } \varphi_k(a_i) = e_S \in S_M \\
        \alpha_{k-1}(m_i, \mathtt{map}(\varphi_{k-1} \circ  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A})(a_i)) &\text{ if } \varphi_k(a_i) = (m_i,a_i) \in S_M.
    \end{cases}
    $$
    By the induction hypothesis
    $
    \alpha_{k-1}(m_i, \mathtt{map}(\varphi_{k-1} \circ  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A})(a_i)) 
    = (\varphi_{k-1} \circ  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A})(m_i, a_i)
    $
    and we can write
    $$
    r_i = (\varphi_{k-1} \circ  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A})(\varphi_k(a_i)) = (\varphi_{k-1} \circ  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A} \circ \varphi_{k-1})(a_i)
    $$
    using \cref{lem:adddepth}.
    Retracing our steps, we now compute
    \begin{align*}
        \alpha_k(m, \mathtt{map}(\varphi_k)(\ell))
        &= (m,(r_i)_i)\\
        &= (m, (\varphi_{k-1} \circ  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A} \circ \varphi_{k-1})(a_i)_i)\\
        &= (m, \mathtt{map}(\varphi_{k-1}) (( 
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A} \circ \varphi_{k-1})(a_i))_i)\\
        &= \varphi_k(\alpha(m,  ( 
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A} \circ \varphi_{k-1})(a_i))_i  ))\\
        &= (\varphi_k \circ  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A} \circ \varphi_k)(\alpha(m, (a_i)_i ))\\
        &= \varphi_k(\alpha(m, \ell))
    \end{align*}
    using that $\varphi$ is a measuring twice.
    We conclude $\varphi_k \colon A \to S_{M,k}$ is an algebra morphism for all $0 \leq k \leq n$.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:AtoS_nunique}
    For any $S_{M,n}^\circ$-initial algebra $A$, there exist at most one algebra morphism $A \to S_{M,n}$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
By \cref{prop:map from initial alg to dual}, there exists a unique morphism $A \to [S_{M,n}^\circ, S_{M}]$ for any $S_{M,n}^\circ$-initial algebra $A$.
    Since $S_{M,n}$ is $S_{M,n}^\circ$-initial we know there exists a unique morphism $\iota \colon S_{M,n} \rightarrowtail [S_{M,n}^\circ, S_{M}]$.
         
    This map is given by
    \begin{align*}
        \iota \colon S_{M,n} &\to [S_{M,n}^\circ, S_{M}] \\
        e_S &\mapsto \operatorname{const}_{e_S}\\
        (m,\ell) &\mapsto
        \left( 
        s' \mapsto 
        \begin{cases}
            e_S &\text{ if } s' = e_S \\
            (m'\bullet m, \mathtt{map}(\iota)(\mathtt{zip}(\ell,\ell'))) &\text{ if } s' = (m', \ell').
        \end{cases}
        \right).
    \end{align*}
    We can easily conclude $\iota$ is a monomorphism by observing that $\iota(s)(s_n) = s$ for all $s \in S_{M,n}$.
    Given any two morphisms $f,g\colon A \to S_{M,n}$, we can draw the following diagram
    \[\begin{tikzcd}
        A & {[S_{M,n}^\circ, S_{M}]} \\
        & S_{M,n}
        \arrow["{!}", from=1-1, to=1-2]
        \arrow["f"', shift right, from=1-1, to=2-2]
        \arrow["g", shift left, from=1-1, to=2-2]
        \arrow["\iota"', tail, from=2-2, to=1-2].
    \end{tikzcd}\]
    Since the morphism $A \to [S_{M,n}^\circ, S_{M}]$ is unique, we know the composites $\iota \circ f = \iota \circ g$, and by $\iota$ being mono we conclude $f = g$.
    Hence, there can be at most one algebra morphism from a $S_{M,n}^\circ$-initial algebra $A$ to $S_{M,n}$.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- theorem-13: body_md -->
The algebra $S_{M,n}$ is the terminal $S_{M,n}^\circ$-initial algebra.
<!-- end theorem-13 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
Given an $S_{M,n}^\circ$-initial algebra $A$, by  \cref{prop:AtoS_nexists}, we obtain an algebra morphism $\varphi_n \colon A \to S_{M,n}$.
    By \cref{lem:AtoS_nunique}, it is unique.
    We conclude $\mathbb{n}$ is the terminal $S_{M,n}^\circ$-initial algebra.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
